2022-2023

RANDALL L. BRILL
Grand Master
October 23, 2022 - October 29, 2023

ii

Brother Randall Louis Brill was raised a Master Mason in San Diego
Lodge No. 35 on September 9, 2005. He served as master of the lodge in 2009.
Brother Brill was elected Grand Master at the last Annual Communication
and has served in a number of roles over the last decade. He was appointed
grand chaplain in 2012. He served on the Fraternal Support Services committee,
Institute for Masonic Studies, Masonic Education committee, and the Public
Schools Advisory Council for which he was the San Diego chairman. Brother
Brill acted as a facilitator for Grand Lodge leadership retreats and the Inspector
Development Academy, serving as the chairman of the program and of a recent
task force to reorganize it. For six years, Brother Brill served as a trustee for the
California Masonic Foundation and has been an integral leader in the Let’s Write
the Future Campaign, as well as on the board of the Nob Hill Masonic Center,
the California Masonic Foundation, Acacia Creek and the Masonic Homes of
California.
In addition to this service, Brother Brill is active in several Masonic
Organizations. He is a 33° Inspector General Honorary in the Scottish Rite
Valley of San Diego. He served as venerable master of the Lodge of Perfection
in 2012 and served as general secretary of the Valley for ten years, from 2009
to 2019. He is a member of San Diego Chapter No. 61 Royal Arch Masons, San
Diego Council No. 23 Cryptic Masons, and San Diego Commandery No. 25
Knights Templar. He has been a member of the Al Bahr Shrine since 2008.
Brother Brill was a member of Inkopah Council No. 86 Allied Masonic Degrees
and served as sovereign master in 2012. He a past puissant sovereign of the
San Diego Conclave Red Cross of Constantine and a member of the Southern
California Rosicrucian College.
Brother Brill received a Ph.D. in experimental psychology from Loyola
University in Chicago. After four years of teaching science and math at a private
school in Illinois, he began a long career in marine mammal training and research
that led to research and leadership assignments around the globe. In 1975, he
was a marine mammal trainer and training supervisor for the Chicago Zoological
Society. After proving that dolphins use their lower jaws to hear returning
echolocations signals, he went on to serve as a scientist and branch head of the
Scientific and Veterinary Support Branch of the U.S. Marine Mammal Program,

ONE HUNDRED SEVENTY FOURTH
ANNUAL COMMUNICATION
Friday Afternoon, October 27, 2023
The 174th Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted
Masons of the State of California was called to order by Grand Master Randall
L. Brill on Friday, October 27, 2023.
Worshipful Brother Gerry C. Craft, master of San Diego Lodge No. 35,
raised the grand lodge during the opening session using a gavel in the shape of
a dolphin, presented to the grand master by that lodge at a reception on June
16, 2023.
Reception of the Past Grand Masters
The grand master welcomed the brethren and directed the grand marshal to
present the past grand masters of the Grand Lodge of California at the altar. The
grand marshal then introduced each past grand master, and the grand master
and deputy grand master personally greeted each one. The grand master asked
the brethren to join him in saluting our past grand masters by the battery of
three times three. The past grand masters were then escorted to seats reserved
for them in the auditorium. The grand master then directed the grand secretary
to send to each absent past grand master the usual letter of greeting from the
grand lodge.
Roll Call
The grand secretary was asked to call the roll of grand lodge officers, past grand
masters, and past grand officers, and to ascertain if a constitutional number
were present to convene the Grand Lodge of California. The following were
present as indicated by their response to the calling of the roll:

None present
The grand secretary announced that, according to the credentials report,
there were 1,003 Master Masons registered as of 12 p.m. Friday, with at least
20 percent of the lodges chartered by this grand lodge represented, and that
therefore a quorum was present as required for the transaction of business.
The grand secretary reported that all lodges had paid their annual per capita
assessment to grand lodge.
Grand Lodge Opening
The grand master then opened grand lodge in ancient form. The grand marshal
and the deacons retired to escort the flag of the United States of America into
the auditorium, which was followed by the pledge of allegiance.
Introductions
The following were asked to rise as groups for recognition:
Residents of the Masonic Homes and Acacia Creek, Diamond Jubilee Award
recipients, Golden Veteran Award recipients, Hiram Award recipients, worshipful masters, lodge secretaries, officer’s coaches, constitutional board members,
grand lodge committeemen, and district inspectors. Each group was greeted
with a round of applause.
The grand master also recognized grand lodge officers visiting from other
jurisdictions.
Reception of Visiting Grand Masters
The grand master then directed the grand marshal to escort the visiting grand
masters from sister jurisdictions into the auditorium. The following were
received with private grand honors and introduced:

Grand Master’s Message
The grand master then relinquished his chair to the deputy grand master for
the purpose of delivering the grand master’s message (Appendix A). After his
message, the grand master received a standing ovation and resumed his station.
Grand Treasurer’s Report
The grand master called on the grand treasurer, Very Worshipful Charles P.
Cross, for his report (Appendix D).
Report of the Grand Secretary
The grand master called on the grand secretary, Very Worshipful Allan L.
Casalou, for his report (Appendix E).
Report of the Grand Lecturer
The grand master called on the grand lecturer, Very Worshipful Ricky L. Lawler,
for his report (Appendix F).
Video Presentation from the
California Masonic Memorial Temple Board of Trustees
The grand master directed attention to the video screen for the Report of the
California Masonic Memorial Temple Board of Trustees. The complete written
reports of both boards can be found in Appendix J of these proceedings.
Legislation
The grand master called on the chairman of the jurisprudence committee, David
M. Ferreria, for his report (Appendix K).
The grand master then called on the chairman of the finance committee,
Levon H. Keshishian, for his report (Appendix K).
The grand master instructed the members of the established rules governing the proper protocol and manner of discussion on the various pieces of
legislation and proceeded with the legislation starting with Grand Master’s
Decision and Recommendation.

At 4:32 p.m., the grand master called grand lodge from labor to refreshment,
to be called on again on Saturday at 8:30 a.m.

Saturday Morning, October 28, 2023
The Grand Lodge of California convened at 8:35 a.m. and, after prayer
by the grand chaplain, the grand master noted that grand lodge was raised by
Worshipful Brother Jon G. Rick, master of Consuelo Lodge No. 325, using a
gavel presented to the grand master by the San Jose Scottish Rite at a reception
on July 11, 2023.
Introduction of the District Inspectors
The grand master then directed the grand marshal to escort the district inspectors into the auditorium. The grand master thanked the inspectors for their
continued service to the fraternity and presented each of them with a small token
of appreciation. The grand master asked the brethren to join him in saluting
our district inspectors by the battery of three times three.
Video Presentation from the Masonic Homes Board of Trustees
The grand master directed attention to the video screen for the Report of the
Masonic Homes Board of Trustees. The complete written report can be found
in Appendix J of these proceedings.
Memorial Service
The grand master called on the Very Reverend Ralph C. Shelton II, grand chaplain, to present a service of remembrance for our departed brethren. His remarks
were as follows:
My brothers, we pause now in the character of Masons to remember our
worthy brothers called from earthly labor to take their stations in the celestial lodge during the past year. Let us join in a moment of remembrance and
appreciation of their lives and their brotherhood, knowing that they labored
to fulfill the obligations they undertook willingly and joyfully. Let each of us
reflect on those who have passed. Consider the impact they had on your life
and the lives of those around them. Some were mentors or coaches. Some
were leaders, others reliable followers. Perhaps you are thinking of a brother
with whom you just enjoyed monthly dinner. We are all here because we have
been called to service, and we know that we will one day be called from labor
to refreshment, just as our departed brothers have been, with labor to resume
on a degree as yet unknown to us.
We are reminded that what we do for ourselves is fleeting, but what we do

12

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

for others lives on. We mourn the passing of our departed and celebrate their
memory. Let us also honor them in our lives each day, build on their example,
add our contribution to theirs. Each departing brother represents a loss, of
course, but also an opportunity to live in their honor. One day our names will
be recited by brothers who still labor as they gather at the festive board, and we
can only hope to be remembered as fondly as those who we remember today.
On the passing of a friend, Benjamin Franklin recorded his thoughts on
the transition from this chapter to the next in a letter to a colleague. In his
words, “We are spirits. That bodies should have lent us, while they can afford
us pleasure, assist us in acquiring knowledge, or in doing good to our fellow
creatures, is a kind and benevolent act of God. When they become unfit for these
purposes and afford us pain instead of pleasure, instead of an aid become an
encumbrance, and answer none of the intentions for which they were given, it
is equally kind and benevolent, that a way is provided by which we may get rid
of them. Death is that way. Our friend and we were invited abroad on a party
of pleasure, which is to last forever. His chair was ready first and he has gone
before us. We could not all conveniently start together; and why should you and
I be grieved at this, since we are soon to follow, and know where to find him.”
We know where to find our brothers, at that eternal festive board to which
Worshipful Franklin refers, and we live to be worthy of admission to that gathering. Please join me in prayer.
Supreme grand master, we thank you for the brotherhood we have been
honored to share with those who have completed their Earthly journey and
commend them to your loving care. We ask that you look on us with favor and
grace as we continue to toil and pray that your wisdom and guidance will lead
us, when the time comes, to the celestial lodge where you forever hold the
gavel. Until then, bless us and keep us, and inspire us to live in harmony and
in peace. Amen.
The grand master thanked the grand chaplain and noted that two past grand
masters laid down their trowels and ended their earthly toils: Most Worshipful
Brother David C. Decker, and Most Worshipful Brother Frederick L. Sorsabal.

The grand master called on Most Worshipful Brother Larry L. Adamson to
deliver the eulogy for Most Worshipful Brother David C. Decker. His remarks
were as follows:

He also made nursing chow for cows with calves, cat chow, and the heralded monkey chow. What made this job so desirable was that the lab unit staff
were required to taste every batch to decide if it was just right. David’s favorite,
monkey chow!
Most worshipful decided that he would take a break from monkey chow
and enlisted in the United States Air Force, where he spent a majority of his
duty in Greenland in a technical communication support unit. Returning to
civilian life, he worked for General Electric and then for General Telephone.
That career spanned 27 years with him retiring in 1991.
Most Worshipful David met Nancy in 1960 and they married in May of
1962. While on a journey to the beach, they exited in Upland for a quick drink
and they both loved what they saw and decided to make Upland their home.
Most Worshipful David joined Freemasonry in 1966 after being encouraged by one of his fellow workers at the telephone company. He joined Upland
Lodge, now Upland Mt. Baldy No. 419. He remained loyal to that lodge his
entire Masonic career. He served as master of his lodge in 1974 and in 2000 was
installed as the 136th grand master of Masons in California.
I had the distinguished honor to serve with him that year as his grand orator.
But 23 days before his grand lodge session was scheduled to begin in 2001, the
horrendous events of September 11 occurred and both he and I immediately
spoke and began to rethink the messaging that we were to deliver at those sessions. It was difficult for Most Worshipful David because he was so filled with
optimism and positivity in everything he did and said. We agreed that I would
deliver the strong condemnation message and he, in keeping with his persona,
would concentrate on the positive feelings of patriotism and community.
Most Worshipful Decker laid down his working tools on April 8 of this year,
four days after his 86th birthday. Our brotherhood lost a great Mason and for
those of us who were close to him, we lost an even greater friend. It’s only fitting
that I conclude by saying, “Until we meet again my brother, we know that you
are in comfort in the palm of God’s hands.”

Eulogy
David C. Decker
May the Road rise up to meet you,
May the Wind be always at your back.
May the Sun shine warn upon your face,
And the Rain fall soft upon your fields.
Until we meet again,
May God hold you in the palm of his hands.
That was the way the Most Worshipful David Decker ended all of
his messages as our grand master because this limerick personified the person
that most worshipful was in his life. No pretense, no fanfare; just genuine and
sincere affection for his fellow man. That was the essence of our brother David.
Most Worshipful David Charles Decker was the youngest of two children
born in 1937 in the windy city of Chicago, the same city as our Grand Master.
His father was in the United States Army and was a training officer charged
with teaching rifle use and maintenance. As such, the family followed him in his
multiple assignments, moving every six or so months to different base locations.
As such, David struggled to establish early childhood friendships.
As a teenager, he lived on the family farm, riding a horse bareback from the
farmhouse to the neighbor’s farm where he boarded the horse and then jumped
onto a yellow school bus for the rest of the ride to school.
David was very athletic and during his high school years he lettered in every
sport his high school offered. He didn’t, however, letter in football—not because
he wouldn’t have been a great player, but because they didn’t have students to
field a team. You see, his graduating class in 1955 consisted of eight.
I share this because it formed the foundation for the person that David
became. It was those formative years that guided his deep respect for a valued-based life and taught him the importance of respect, responsibility, and
integrity.
David’s professional life has some true intrigue and fascination built into
it. Moving away from the country and back to the city, he landed a job with
the Eagle Signal Company making traffic signals. It didn’t take long for him to
realize that making red, yellow, and green lighted signals wouldn’t be his life’s
endeavor, so he embarked on a unique job opportunity that he didn’t readily
share with most of us that were part of his peer group.
Dog food! Yes, dog food with Ralston Purina, where he was part of the
prestigious experimental lab unit making various animal feed. David’s claim to
fame was his unit’s development of the famed Purina Dog Chow.

Eulogy
Frederick L. Sorsabal

Frederick L. Sorsabal
Grand Master 2005-2006
Placerville Lodge No. 26
July 24, 1937 – July 22, 2023

Frederick Louis Sorsabal was born on July 24, 1937 in Fullerton, California,
the third son of Earma and Andrew J Sorsabal, Sr. His family are Basque, and
he was raised eating their food and hearing their stories. He was very proud
to be Basque.
He attended school in Fullerton, including Fullerton Community College,
before going to California State University Long Beach, where he graduated with
a bachelor of sciences degree in political science with an emphasis in public
administration. Before graduating from high school, he worked many odd jobs,
the best of which was working at Disneyland on opening day in 1955. The most
important thing to happen to Fred also happened while he was at Fullerton
High, when he met Marlene. They have been an item ever since.
Fred was busy as a bee, working and going to college, but he found time
to marry Marlene on July 25, 1958. They have two sons, six grandchildren, and
two great-grandchildren.
During his senior year at Long Beach, with the help of a favorite professor, he
became interested in city management while interning with the city of Anaheim.
Shortly after graduation, he started working full-time with the city in the city
manager’s office. He worked there until 1968, when he accepted a position with
the city of San Bernardino as the assistant city administrator. He stayed in San
Bernardino for only a short time and came back to Orange County as the assistant city manager for the city of Costa Mesa in 1969. In 1970, he was appointed
city manager of Costa Mesa, where he stayed until he retired for the first time
in 1985. During his time in Costa Mesa, the development of South Coast Plaza
Shopping Center and Orange County Music Center were completed. At the
time, the shopping center was the largest west of the Mississippi.
Fred’s first retirement was short-lived. In 1986, he was very busy as potentate of El Bekal Shrine. In 1987, after helping Marlene too much around the
house, he “decided to go back to work” and started a consulting business. In
1988, he went back into public service as the city manager of El Segundo, next
to LAX in L.A. County. From there, he became the first full-time city manager
of the new city of Mission Viejo back in Orange County. Fred served at that
post until April 1995, when he retired with Marlene’s blessings. He served in
public management in California for 34 years. Despite his many of years of
public service, he hated to go over bridges or through tunnels or over anything
too high. He always claimed that what caused his fear was that they were built
by the lowest bidder.
Fred’s oldest brother, Andrew J Sorsabal, Jr., joined Azure Masonic Lodge

18

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

19

No. 533 in 1951, the same year Fred joined Fullerton DeMolay Chapter, which
was sponsored by that lodge. He was master councilor in 1954. Marlene joined
Fullerton Bethel No. 13 of the International Order of Job’s Daughters during
the same time and was honored queen. As an adult, she was bethel guardian.
They have both been active supporters of Masonic youth groups their entire
lives. Fred was honored by DeMolay International with the Legion of Honor
for his many years of service and support.
While working for the city of Anaheim, Fred joined his older brother’s
lodge, Azure No. 533, and was raised by his brother in 1963. Fred joined many
concordant and appendant Masonic organizations, including the Scottish Rite,
York Rite, and the Shrine. Later in his life, the Scottish Rite honored him with
the 33rd degree for his many years of service. He was very active in the El Bekal
Shrine Temple in Anaheim working through the chairs to become the potentate
in 1986.
Fred was very involved in his communities. He volunteered with the
United Way of Orange County, serving with them either as a loaned executive
or on the board of directors; he served on the Girl Scout Council of Orange
County; was one of the founding board members of the Orange County Heart
Association–South Orange County Chapter; he served as president of the City
Manager’s Association of Orange County; was a member of the Mission Hospital
Foundation; coached his sons’ sports teams and was on two exchange programs
for city managers—one to England and the other to Russia right after the fall
of communism.
After Fred finished his term as potentate, he was appointed to the board
of governors of the Shriners for Children Los Angeles Hospital. He served nine
years on the board, three as chairman. He served on the board of the Long
Beach Scottish Rite Language Disorder Clinic and was president of its board.
Fred also became more active in his Masonic lodge. He served as master of
Azure Lodge in 1990. In 1992, he began his direct service to the Grand Lodge of
California as grand orator for Most Worshipful R. Stephen Doan. He served on
the Masonic Speakers Committee and on the board of trustees of the Masonic
Homes of California, include as president of the board. He also served on the
warden’s leadership training retreat’s staff and was chair for three years. Fred
was always the life of any party, the first one on the dance floor and the last
one to leave. He always tried to make sure that everyone was having as good a
time as he was.
In 1995, after Fred retired, and while he was very active in grand lodge
activities, he and Marlene moved from Orange County to Placerville in Northern
California. He promptly joined El Dorado Lodge No. 26 in Placerville and
affiliated with Ben Ali Shrine Temple in Sacramento. Both he and Marlene
volunteered every week at the Shrine Hospital in Sacramento, something they
did until they moved to Idaho in 2019. He also became active in his new lodge
as an officer and served on the building association, including as its president.
He also served on the Marshall Hospital Foundation in Placerville. El Dorado

Lodge awarded him the Hiram Award for service to the lodge in 2000. Still
busy as a bee.
In 2001, Fred was elected junior grand warden of the Grand Lodge of
California and progressed through the line to be elected and installed the 141st
grand master of Masons in California in 2005. Fred was elected as the chairman
of the Conference of Grand Masters of North America in 2006, a huge honor.
After serving as grand master, he continued to sit on the youth orders committee, the legislative analysis committee, and as president of the Institute for
Masonic Studies. He was selected to serve as the personnel representative of
SGIG in California for the Valley of Sacramento.
In 2019, Fred and Marlene moved to Coeur d’Alene, Idaho to be near one
of their sons, grandchildren, and a great-grandchild. Fred joined the local lodge
and other Masonic organizations. Fred loved to use his snow blower and would
always help remove snow for his neighbors. And, of course, he loved to walk
his dog, Bunny. A busy bee to the end.
Most Worshipful Sorsabal selected the Beehive as his symbol when he was
grand master. He introduced it to the craft in his first speech as grand master:
“The Beehive is a Masonic symbol of industry and cooperation. It is a
symbol of social obligation, reciprocal love, and friendship. It is seen in the
harmonious working together of many units to a single end, and reciprocal love
and friendship in the fact that in the most crowded hive, bees live in peace and
harmony with their fellows.
“A bee is a hard and tireless worker, not for himself but for the swarm. It
works in complete cooperation and does so without dissension and lives in a
society ruled by order. Man must work as a unit to accomplish great things.
The builders of old worked as a unit to build those great cathedrals. They could
not work alone and expect to build the mighty edifice. We, as Masons, must
imitate the bee, be industrious, work with others and for others, take pride in
our vocations, obey the rules of our society, and strive to add to our body of
knowledge and understanding. Otherwise, we are useless members of society.”
I believe that this is a perfect description of what Fred believed and how
he tried to live his life.
Fred lived his life following the Masonic principles of the beehive. He was
a great husband, father, grandfather, friend, and brother. He has planted so
many seeds of goodness, love, and friendship that they will be inspiring people
for generations. Our lives are better for having known him and the world is a
better place for having had him in it. I will dearly miss my little buddy. He was
a very busy bee.

Introduction of the New Chief Executive Officer
of the Masonic Homes of California
The grand master, while the grand lodge was still at refreshment, took the
opportunity to highlight a change in the leadership of the Masonic Homes of
California. He informed the brethren that for the past 10 years, our Masonic
Homes were led by Worshipful Brother Gary Charland as president and chief
executive officer. Earlier this year, Most Worshipful Brother Larry L. Adamson,
the chairman of the board of trustees of the Masonic Homes of California, was
informed by Brother Charland of his intent to retire by the end of this year. That
notification prompted the board of trustees to initiate an extensive nationwide
search for a new chief executive officer.
After diligent effort from the board of trustees, in July this year we were
pleased to welcome Terry Quigley as the new leader of our Masonic Homes.
The grand master called on Most Worshipful Brother Adamson, chairman
of the board of trustees of the Masonic Homes of California, to introduce Terry
Quigley to the fraternity. Below are his remarks:
On behalf of the board of trustees of the Masonic Homes of California, I am
pleased to introduce you to Terry Quigley, MSW, NHA, the new chief executive
officer and president of the Masonic Homes of California.
An extensive national search for a chief executive officer enabled us to
identify a proven industry leader who has the experience, vision, and passion
consistent with the practices and principles of California Freemasonry. She is
building upon the organizational vision and leading the future strategic direction
that Gary Charland has erected over the past decade.
Terry is an accomplished leader steeped in building high-trust relationships,
innovative services, and growth at mission-driven human service organizations
like ours. From 2012 until joining the Masonic Homes of California, she was
the chief operating officer at Episcopal Communities and Services in Southern
California, where she oversaw three CCRCs, one assisted living community,
and one affordable housing community together serving roughly 700 residents.

There, she developed three master plans, including the launch of a new 206unit facility; delivered consistent financial performance; and drove excellent
resident satisfaction and engagement in all life plan communities, among other

Prior to 2012, Terry led operations at Shea Family Care and the Cloisters
of La Jolla Skilled Nursing Facility. As a part of a home- and community-based

Her experience as a skilled and respected executive in senior health care,

He is a past celebrant of the California College Masonic Societas
Rosicruciana and has served as its secretary and treasurer. Currently, he is
serving as the chief adept for all California colleges and was recently installed as
the treasurer general for the High Council and received the Knight Grand Cross.
He served his community as scout master for Boy Scout Troup No. 150 in

Nicholas, 30; and Michelle, 27.
Brother Ara is an avid photographer, philatelist, and has a passion for collecting rare antique Masonic books. In his spare time, he enjoys visiting national
parks, backpacking, camping in the High Sierras, reading, and listening to music.

Ara Maloyan Biography
Worshipful Brother Ara Maloyan was raised a Master Mason in Hayastan
Lodge No. 94 in the District of Columbia, where he remains a life member.
He affiliated with Santa Monica Palisades Lodge No. 307 in California in
2000 and served as master of that lodge in 2005. He served six years as treasurer of the lodge and currently serves as a trustee, and in 2015, the lodge
recognized him with the Hiram Award. He is also a past master of George
Washington Lodge No. 4 under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of Armenia.
After graduating from California State University Los Angeles with a bachelor of
sciences in civil and structural engineering, Brother Ara obtained his California
civil engineering license and began a career with city of Los Angeles in 1984,
specializing in earthquake mitigation of unreinforced masonry buildings. In
1989, Brother Ara went to work for the city of Beverly Hills in different capacities, culminating with his last position as city engineer overseeing design and
construction of the city’s multimillion-dollar infrastructure. He then served as
director of public works and as city engineer for the city of Long Beach and as

Presentation of the Joe Jackson Award
This year, the Masonic Homes of California and our grand lodge were pleased
to present an award in memory of our late brother Joe Jackson.
Joe Jackson, a Mason for 60 years and Hiram Award recipient, served Joseph
L. Shell Daylight Lodge No. 837 and Heartland Lodge No. 576 for 17 years as
secretary, assistant secretary, treasurer, and chaplain.
Joe exemplified Masonic relief and brotherly love. He reached out to members and widows on a weekly basis, assisted with numerous applications to
MOS and the Masonic Homes, frequently called Masonic Assistance to check
the status of his member’s applications, and helped expedite the paperwork
process. He connected members and their families not only to Masonic services
but also to community resources and programs for veterans. If Joe Jackson was
involved in providing relief, the outcome was guaranteed to be a positive one.
Through his tireless efforts and determination to improve and grow outreach, Joe was a catalyst for launching the successful lodge outreach strategic
initiative in Division IX. Joe passed away in 2012, leaving a legacy that set the

Miss California Job’s Daughters
Grand master, distinguished guests, and Masons of California, hello! My name
is Erica McHorney, and I am your Miss California Job’s Daughter for 2023–2024.
I proudly come from over five generations of Masonic heritage dating back
through my mother’s family. My job is to travel around the state and speak to
our adult Masonic family about Job’s Daughters. I’d like to congratulate this
year’s officers on a job well done. Your dedication to our youth orders does not
go unnoticed. To the incoming officers, I am excited for the incredible work
you gentlemen will do this coming year.
Today, I stand before you to speak about a connection, a bond, and an
alignment of values that unites our two esteemed organizations. The journey of
Job’s Daughters is deeply intertwined with the values of the Masonic family. Our
core principles are not just similar; they complement each other, strengthening
the bond between our organizations.
Freemasonry teaches the importance of brotherly love—of supporting one
another in both good times and bad. Job’s Daughters, too, instills the value of
sisterhood among its members, creating lifelong bonds that stand the test of
time. Together, we are reminded that while our journey in life is personal, we
never walk alone.
Our teachings of personal growth and education have an incredible impact
on the members of our orders. Freemasonry encourages its members to seek
light, knowledge, and self-improvement. Job’s Daughters similarly focuses on
equipping its members with the tools they need to succeed in life. Both of our
institutions understand that growth is a lifelong journey, and we are committed
to guiding our members every step of the way. You are all specially equipped
to support and foster those in our youth organizations who are growing as
leaders and as people.
Job’s Daughters International is uniquely positioned to cultivate strong
leaders. Our organization entrusts young women with responsibilities, nurturing

their capabilities and helping them grow in their roles. Similarly, Freemasonry

the world. We are taught to be selfless, to lend a hand to those in need, and to
dedicate our lives to the service of others.
The Masonic family is a beacon of hope in our communities, one that has
made an impact throughout history and will continue to do so.
The values of Job’s Daughters and the Masonic family might have been

Miss Hannah Ray, Grand Worthy Advisor
International Order of Rainbow
Most Worshipful Grand Master Brill, officers, and members of grand lodge,
Distinguished and honored guests and friends of California Rainbow, hello!
I’m honored to be with you all here today in beautiful San Francisco and thank
you for the opportunity to speak on behalf of the youth leaders of California
Rainbow. I would like to take a moment to introduce some of my fellow grand
officers who are here today, as well as our state parents for grand assembly 2024.
If you’ve ever been to a live performance, there is almost always live music.
The first time I experienced a Broadway musical in New York, I was blown away
by not only the actors and actresses bringing the story and magic of Disney’s
Frozen to life, but by the incredible orchestra that accompanies the performers.
As someone who has been involved in music since before I could walk and talk,
I’ve grown to appreciate just how important music is in order to bring a story
to life—and perhaps more importantly, the lessons our organizations can learn
from their harmony. Some might even say that music is magic.
Now, with all this talk of live music, you might be wondering why I’m
holding instruments in my hands. Unfortunately, it is not to serenade you. This
is an egg shaker and this is a tambourine. Though they are both percussion
instruments, they still have their own unique sound even though they come
from the same family. If I shake both of these instruments at the same time,
it’s loud and chaotic, lacking both direction and melody. But, when I give these
two instruments a purpose, allow their individual sounds to be heard, and use
them in a specific way, we can utilize each of their unique tones to create music.
This weekend, many of you were introduced, or reintroduced, to Mozart’s
The Magic Flute, a fairy tale of darkness, light, and finding your way in the world.
The principal characters, Prince Tamino and Papageno, are each given magical
instruments to aid in their search for the queen of the night’s daughter, Pamina.
The duo utilize these instruments to the best of their abilities, and with the help
of some magic, Tamino is successfully reunited with Pamina.
However, if the instruments weren’t used in a way to create music, and
there wasn’t an openness to the value of the magic that each of the instruments
held, there would have only been noise, and no progress would be made, and
Pamina may not have ever been rescued.
Like Tamino and Papageno and these two instruments, we as Masonic
organizations have a responsibility to find harmony in our values and goals. We
strive to recognize our strengths, our “magic,” and use them in a way that will

36

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

37

benefit our world—similar to the Magic Flute’s premise. But, despite the aspirations that we all share, we often fall short of working together to achieve them.
Rather than actively listening to one another and truly paying attention without
interruption or being receptive to their ideas, we are like the chaotic sounds
of the egg shaker and tambourine. Rather than cohesive, the communication
between us becomes chaotic, competitive, and sometimes even self-centered.
Ask yourself: “If the Masonic family were a symphony, would we be playing
together as in harmony, or would each of our beautiful and unique music be
lost in a chaotic mess of sound?” If I were to answer today, I would lean toward
the mess. But as I reflect on the story of Tamino and Papageno, as well as my
own deep appreciation for music, I know that we can find our shared song and
create a Masonic symphony.
An instrument is only as good as the person who plays it, and a symphony
is only as good as the people in it. Our organizations can, and should, work
together to achieve growth and prosperity. But if we are not willing to listen to
each other and hear what each of our orders have to contribute to our Masonic
symphony, we will find our story slows its progress.
For example: Our youth orders have continuously been voicing their need
for support from the adult orders, and members of the adult orders have been
voicing their desire for younger members to join their lodges and chapters. In
failing to truly listen to each other, we believe that these needs are at odds.
But in reality they are all derived from the same truth—the need to grow our
organizations. Think how much further the sound of our Masonic symphony
would reach if we worked together in harmony to build membership, create
retention programs, and share the incredible opportunities our organizations
provide worldwide.
California Rainbow has been working hard to keep our musical family
thriving and working together. Utilizing our strengths, we’ve been working to
hold fun membership events, fundraisers like our Grand Service Project that
we raised over $72,000 for last year, and our statewide canned food drive in
an effort to see our organization flourish. My question to all of you is, how can
you get involved with Rainbow? How can you work with not only Rainbow, but
DeMolay and Job’s Daughters to create harmony amongst our jurisdictions?
Will it be joining an advisory board? Attending regular meetings and events?
Introducing Rainbow to a lodge that has no active youth?
How can the youth better understand you? What do you want to see from
us to encourage you to participate in our programming? How can we be supporting each other equally in an effort to achieve progress for all? My challenge
to all of you is to work together with your lodges to create harmony between
our organizations. If we can begin to actively listen to one another and reunite
as a Masonic family, we can create beautiful, symphonic melodies that will last
for years to come.
Thank you once again Most Worshipful Grand Master Brill for inviting me
to speak to you today, and we hope to see many of you again at our Waves of

Opportunity Lie Beyond the Shore in 2024 Grand Assembly sessions, which
will be held in Visalia from March 23–26. Thank you.
Mr. Jody Williams, Master Councilor
Southern California, DeMolay International

As many young men start out, their lives are a jumble of new and different
interests, all hopefully leading reasonably rapidly toward some final decision
as to what special purpose life might have in store for them. Well, for me, that
did not happen easily.
It took a very long time to get serious about putting some meaning and
desire into a proper perspective for me. After 26 years of following my own
whims and curiosity, it took an attractive young lady, my wife, coming into
my life to make me realize that I might go beyond myself and my own wants,

and begin to try to orient my personal goals to the betterment of the world
around me.
She got me away from a limited midwestern surrounding and out to
California, where I saw my capabilities greatly expand, and most happily found
very interesting opportunities to work and serve with others. And it eventually
became clear to me that providing service and assuring a well-done activity
made me feel much better than just pushing for personal gain.
But it took another 20 years for Masonry and me to meet each other!
Notwithstanding that my father, grandfather, uncles, and other relatives were
all Masons, little was said to me about it back in my early days, and so I had little
interest then. However, it was my daughter joining the Masonic youth order of
Job’s Daughters that you all saw honored here earlier this morning that finally
brought me into this fraternity.
Once that I took that first step as a Mason, I really found that this organization and its ideals provided what to me was an extremely positive environment
toward personal improvement as a human being.
I am very certain that these ideals have been a strong influence in developing
my talents toward making my activities worthwhile to others, and in guiding
my many various activities and support services in Masonry for all these years.
Serving this fraternity as an inspector since 1990 has been my favorite activity, and I hope that my guidance and assistance to at least 12 separate lodges in
the Los Angeles area has been helpful. I am still serving in a support role as an
inspector-at-large at this time.
Of course, assisting our 1998 Grand Master Melville Nahin as his grand
marshal was a labor of love and something I still cherish deeply.
And my current charitable service to the fraternity, leading the Los Angeles
Masonic Service Bureau as its executive secretary for the past 15 years, has been
most meaningful to me.
So, as a Mason, I have therefore always tried to serve and act with love and
understanding toward others, as I believe all mankind should interact with one
another. Would that this whole world be following our Masonic principles!
Even as late as I began my Masonic journey, I will have been a Mason for 50
years in three more years. It has been one of the finest parts of my life, and any
special recognition of the service and achievements I may have provided pale in
importance to the benefits and pleasure that it has given me over all these years.
Thank you, Masonry. Thank you, Most Worshipful. And thank you all.

REPORT OF THE GRAND MASTER
Brethren, the time has come for me to fulfill my constitutional duty by
providing an overview of the state of the craft, my official actions as grand
master, and our accomplishments over the past year.
State of the Fraternity
Despite the setbacks caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, our grand lodge has
demonstrated impressive resilience by not only recovering but thriving. We have
embarked on several new initiatives and are poised for a brighter future that
is filled with harmony and meaningful endeavors. The strength of our fraternity, and our grand lodge in particular, lies in our unwavering commitment to
time-honored traditions and principles of true friendship, inclusivity, harmony,
and our collective dedication to improving our communities and ourselves.
Membership and Degrees
If you have followed the membership trends of our grand lodge, you know that
we were on track for growth in 2020 but the pandemic caused an unexpected
loss of about 200 members during that year. The major setback came in 2021,
when the pandemic continued to disrupt our ability to initiate and affiliate new
members. In addition, we also experienced a substantial increase in suspensions
and deaths resulting in the largest single loss of members in decades, at more
than 4,000 members.
The past two years, however, have shown positive signs of recovery with
lodges keeping applicants and candidates interested and involved, resulting in
our conferring more degrees than immediately prior to the pandemic. Making a
Mason is a significant commitment of time and effort. The same energies must
be invested in retaining new members as well. My heartfelt thanks go out to
those lodges that have contributed to this boon in membership by faithfully
preserving the interest of candidates and members during this time.
In a similar vein, lodges must stay actively connected with delinquent
members and personally reach out to them before considering suspension.
Gaining an understanding of their circumstances, helping when needed, and
ensuring that they are valued by their lodge and this fraternity are paramount.
We should not hesitate to go so far as considering the full or partial remission
of dues for those facing financial difficulty.
Most importantly, it is crucial to acknowledge that relying on a social media

50

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

post or email for communication is insufficient. We are a truly a band of brothers
and communicating by impersonal means alone is sadly insufficient. Nothing has
more impact than personal visits and phone calls. They are essential and most
effective in building strong connections and reinforcing a sense of belonging
within our lodges. By making clear our care and commitment to each member,
we can work together to improve member retention and ensure the continued
growth and strength of our grand lodge.

ensuring the availability of Masonic opportunities for interested individuals
across the state.

Interest in Membership
It is so encouraging to observe that while some Masonic lodges may face challenges in connecting with prospective members, there remains a strong interest in Freemasonry throughout the state. Thanks to our positive awareness
campaign, we have received literally thousands of inquiries about membership,
keeping our dedicated membership advisors hard at work. From these inquiries
they have identified and recorded more than 5,000 qualified prospects this year.
A number of these have become Masons in our grand lodge or another grand
lodge. Some have become inactive for varying reasons. Currently, more than
2,500 prospects are still in our system awaiting contact from lodges that have
been made aware.
It’s encouraging to note that more than half of the lodges have been successful in making these connections. Lodges that have embraced this initiative
have experienced notable success. An example is Old West Lodge No. 813,
which achieved a significant milestone by conferring 26 degrees in the past
year, including 15 Entered Apprentice degrees. Similarly, Culver City Foshay
Lodge No. 467 has shown diligence in engaging prospects resulting in 38 conferrals including 15 Entered Apprentice degrees. The commitment of Acalanes
Fellowship Lodge No. 480 to staying engaged with prospects has also led to
over 20 degrees conferred in the last year. There are so many other lodges that
kept prospects engaged in various ways. That makes it clear that we do have
the capacity and responsibility to welcome them into our lodges.
Lodge Development
For the past seven years, our grand lodge has made it a priority to establish new
lodges, recognizing that lodges play a fundamental role in making and engaging
Masons. This strategic focus is intended to ensure that we have lodges in all
regions of the state where there are enough interested individuals, as well as
in areas of dense population to meet the growing demand. When this initiative
began in 2016, we had 327 lodges. Since then, we have seen 19 lodges undergo
consolidation or dissolution. Without any efforts to create new lodges, we
would currently have 308 lodges. Fortunately, thanks to our successful endeavors in forming new lodges, as of June 30, 2023, we have increased the number
of lodges to 332, with more lodges in development, resulting in a net growth
in the number of lodges since 2016. This demonstrates our commitment to

51

Lodge Leadership
Volunteer leadership within Masonic lodges is an essential pillar of our community engagement. Our lodges serve as crucial community assets, providing a
platform for individuals to gather, enhance personal growth, and make positive
contributions to society. Masons are renowned for their community-mindedness and their readiness to effect positive change. It is no less than a profound
honor to be a volunteer leader within a Masonic lodge. The master of the lodge,
alongside his other lodge and hall officers, make up a vital leadership team. In a
time in our society when fewer individuals are inclined to dedicate their personal
time and resources for the betterment of their community, we began this year
with many more vacancies in lodge offices than normal. However, by spring,
most of these positions had been filled. I thank all of you who have answered the
call for local leadership and I urge all Masons residing near a lodge to seriously
consider the gratifying opportunity of sharing their time and talents as leaders
within our cherished fraternity. Only together can we continue to strengthen
our communities and uphold our noble traditions.

Official Acts
Lodge Suspensions
Nothing has been more difficult and heartbreaking for me this year than to have
been given cause to suspend the charters of six lodges. The suspension of the
charters for Coachella Lodge No. 476 and Palm Springs Lodge No. 693 was the
result of significant deficiencies in administrative and financial matters. In the
case of Coachella Lodge No. 476, the elected lodge officers and hall directors
initially neglected their duties, leading to adverse effects on both the lodge and
its hall. Despite some initial resistance, they eventually recognized the value of
assistance from the inspector and assistant grand lecturer and worked diligently
to address the concerns. Ultimately their efforts led to the reinstatement of
their charter earlier this year and I congratulate them for that.
However, the situation at Palm Springs Lodge No. 693 was different. This
lodge continued to suffer due to a lack of commitment from its leaders, who
neglected their responsibilities. Unfortunately, despite efforts from the inspector
and assistant grand lecturer, many of the active members of this lodge chose
not to cooperate and, instead, appeared to conspire against the lodge’s success.
They refused to provide information and most of the lodge officers resigned
rather than confront the issues. Former lodge leaders held secret meetings and
activities in direct contravention of the suspension order. We all know that
Freemasonry is built on the principles of working together in harmony and

52

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

adhering to traditions and laws. To uphold our values, we must be willing to
compromise, find common ground, and show respect for one another and the
fraternity. It is my hope that the members of Palm Springs Lodge will embrace
these ideals and eventually work toward resolving their challenges. As of now,
their charter remains suspended.
The suspension of the charters of Golden Gate Speranza Lodge No. 30, East
San Diego Lodge No. 561, and Colusa Lodge No. 240 have been enforced due
to their failure to cause their respective hall associations to seek the approval
of the Masonic Properties Committee prior to entering contracts that require
such approval. In my view, the leaders of these lodges and halls were aware of
these requirements but chose to ignore them. Even if they were unaware, it is
their responsibility to be informed. According to our Masonic law, the master
and senior warden are mandated to serve as directors on hall associations owned
by their respective lodges, primarily to ensure proper oversight as shareholders.
Therefore, it is of the utmost importance that these lodge leaders are well-versed
in hall association requirements. To facilitate meeting that requirement, a free
online course within the Lodge Management Certification Program offers the
requisite hall training and is obligatory for all masters and senior wardens. Hall
association directors must actively engage in this training to prevent such lapses
in the future. As of this date, the charter for Golden Gate Speranza Lodge No.
30 has been restored. The two other charters remain suspended.
Valley Lodge No. 135 faced a suspension due to a breach of our obligations
when some of its members translated the esoteric or secret portion of the ritual
into plain English, which was then printed and used in rehearsals and tiled
meetings. When confronted with the suspension, the lodge took responsibility
for the error and promptly rectified the situation by completing the necessary
requirements for restoration. I am pleased to report that the charter of Valley
Lodge No.135 was successfully restored earlier this year, demonstrating the
lodge’s commitment to upholding the sacred traditions and obligations of
Freemasonry.
The most inspiring and meaningful moment I had during this past year
was the opportunity to make a Mason at sight. Brother Nelson Reichman was
terminally ill and nearing the end of his life. His stated longtime desire was to be
made a Mason. His son James, an officer of the Grand Lodge of New York, made
a request to do so through our own Arcadia Lodge. On April 16 of this year, we
all met at Arcadia Lodge. Nelson was wheeled into the lodge room and placed
in front of the altar. He was feeble but lucid. With all officers in their stations,
I placed a chair in front of Nelson, sat down and held his hands. After quietly
giving him a brief explanation of the fraternity and what we were about to do,
I declared him to be a California Mason. I will never forget how he suddenly
became alert, looked up at me and smiled as broad a smile as possible. A few
weeks later, members of Al Malikah Shrine inducted him as well. I attended
Brother Nelson’s memorial service at Arcadia Lodge on September 13. I can
guarantee that those moments will live in my heart and mind for a very long time.

Lodge Constitutions and Dispensations

53

You may have heard the saying, “Grand lodges make new lodges, and lodges
make new Masons.” The role of the grand lodge is pivotal in overseeing and
fostering the growth of Freemasonry within its jurisdiction. Critical to our
growth coming out of the pandemic has been the establishment and constitution
of new California lodges. I take great pride in the fact that during this year we
have constituted four new lodges which received their charters during the last
Annual Communication. These lodges, namely Andres Bonifacio Lodge No. 879,
Ye Olde Cup and Ball Lodge No. 880, Seven Hills Lodge No. 881, and GAT Jose
Rizal Lodge No. 882, are now esteemed constituent lodges under the umbrella
of the Grand Lodge of California. Furthermore, I have exercised my authority
by issuing dispensations for the formation three additional new lodges: Edwin
Sherman Research Lodge, Pilares del Rey Solomon Lodge, and the California
Hispanic and Latin American Research Lodge. These collectively reflect the
grand lodge’s—and my own—commitment to expansion, diversity, and the
perpetuation of Masonic principles.

Priorities And Achievement
Positive Awareness
As the result of the efforts of Ms. Emily Limon and the members of her staff, our
positive awareness campaign has emerged as the cornerstone of grand lodge’s
2025 plan. We recognize that the more people learn about the actual activities
of Freemasons and the true value of membership, the more favorable their
perception of our fraternity becomes. We’ve also learned that most individuals seek information about Freemasonry through personal connections, often
knowing someone who is a Mason whether it be a family member, neighbor, or
colleague. However, Masons still often hesitate to discuss their fraternity even
with their loved ones and peers.
Our positive awareness initiatives follow a dual approach. First, to encourage more Masons to openly discuss their membership within their social circles,
and secondly to present a comprehensive view of the purposes, activities, and
philanthropic efforts of our fraternity to the public. This year, we continued to
promote all our charitable work, both local and statewide, and launched the
#ImAMason social media campaign for the second time. This campaign ran
for two weeks in July on Facebook and Instagram, encouraging our members
to share the value of their Masonic membership. We received over 700 posts
totaling six million views, filling our social media feeds with #ImAMason messages which more than doubled last year’s results. Furthermore, we inspired
other grand lodges around the world to pick up the campaign. Grand lodges
including in Baja California, Mexico, and other Spanish-speaking jurisdictions
created a variation of the program call #SoyMason.

54

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

In addition to all of that, we initiated a 10-week paid social media campaign
in August aiming to reach thousands with content about our fraternity’s purpose,
activities, and charitable endeavors. Not only are we raising positive awareness
across the state, but we are also likely to generate thousands of membership
inquiries. We have discovered that the public tends to remember what they see
when asked about what Freemasons do.
To make the public aware of what we do, we have redoubled our efforts
to establish a strong presence in communities across the state. In addition to
participating in public school events, cornerstone ceremonies, and programs
like Masons4Mitts, we partnered with the California Masonic Foundation to
sponsor a successful community event in San Diego earlier this year. This event
brought together community and charitable leaders to learn more about our
work and, more importantly, explore opportunities for collaboration. It serves
as a model for engaging our communities and building positive awareness of
Freemasonry’s contributions.
The Masons4Mitts program has achieved remarkable milestones in its 12th
year of operation. Notably, we have raised over $1 million for the San Francisco
Giants Community Foundation, our first Major League partner. Additionally,
the cumulative impact of this program, which now also includes collaboration
with the Los Angeles Dodgers, San Diego Padres, and Los Angeles Angels in
Anaheim, has this year surpassed a remarkable total giving of $2 million. These
achievements demonstrate our commitment to making a positive difference in
our communities through philanthropy and collaboration.

The Grand Lodge of California remains committed to fostering collaboration with grand lodges worldwide. We place great importance on our mutual
exchanges with grand lodges in the Western Conference of Masonic Grand
Lodges and participated in its February meeting. In May, we extended our reach
to the international stage by attending the World Conference of Regular Masonic
Grand Lodges. Furthermore, we are proud to uphold the tradition of attending
the Conference of the Three Californias, a longstanding collaboration with the
grand lodges of Baja California and Baja California Sur, which has been ongoing
since 1978. This year we were honored to welcome the Grand Lodge of Iran in
Exile as a participant in this conference, furthering our global connections and
promoting the spirit of unity and fraternity across borders.
Strengthening our relationships with the Prince Hall Grand Lodge and the
Grand Lodge of Iran in Exile holds particular significance for us as our members
visit each other’s tiled meetings and, in the case of the Grand Lodge of Iran in
Exile, even enjoy dual membership. Beyond attending our respective annual
communications, we have engaged in meaningful meetings and social events
with the elected leadership of the grand lodges to foster ongoing connections
and alignment. These bonds have never been stronger.
During this past year we have explored opportunities for further collaboration, particularly regarding one of our most significant endeavors, the Masonic
Homes of California. With expanded capacity and options, the Masonic Homes
will extend its offerings to the Prince Hall Grand Lodge of California and the
Grand Lodge of Iran in Exile and provide even greater opportunities for our
members and their families to access services and care when needed. Details
are being finalized and we will share more information soon as we continue to
work together for the greater good of Masonry in California.
In February, we had the privilege of attending the Conference of Grand
Masters of Masons of North America in Arlington, Virginia. The highlight
of this conference was the commemoration of the 100th anniversary of the
George Washington Masonic National Memorial, which drew thousands of
Masons from across the continent. The Grand Lodge of California was well
represented in a significant and well-attended public parade from downtown
Alexandria to the memorial.
Susan and I were honored to represent you at this momentous event.
Furthermore, it is with great pride that we acknowledge our own past grand
master, Most Worshipful Brother Ken Nagel, who was elected as the president of the memorial for a three-year term. We extend our gratitude to Most
Worshipful Brother Nagel for his dedicated service to this national cause which
holds significant importance for Masons worldwide.

Engagement with Other Grand Lodges
Building strong and collaborative relationships with other grand lodges has
been a top priority for us, especially those operating in California. We are fortunate to have a diverse range of Masonic organizations in our state, offering
opportunities for all individuals of good character to join and participate. Our
objective is to deepen these connections, eliminate barriers to engagement, and
present a comprehensive picture of Freemasonry in California to the public.
In pursuing this goal, we have continued to strengthen our ties with organizations such as the Prince Hall Grand Lodge of California and the Grand Lodge
of Iran in Exile. We also engage other grand lodges like the George Washington
Union Grand Lodge, the Women’s Grand Lodge of California, and Universal
Co-Freemasonry. These organizations charter lodges in California that include
individuals of all genders and backgrounds, providing diverse options for membership and engagement.
It is most essential to clarify that our aim in building bridges with these
various grand lodges is not integration but rather collaboration. We believe that
maintaining separate structures that support different membership options and
traditions makes us collectively stronger. Our ultimate objective is to showcase
the rich tapestry of Freemasonry in California and demonstrate its relevance
and significance in the world.

Masonic Homes
I am happy to recognize the successful completion of the master campus plan
initiated several years ago for the Masonic Homes of California. You will hear
a more detailed report tomorrow, but I can confidently say that Masons of

enhancement of our campuses in both Union City and Covina. Masons and
their family members now can reside on our campuses without the need for
relocation to different communities for higher levels of care. Most importantly,

Working Tools
I am personally very proud to announce the successful launch of a new program
in partnership with the California Masonic Foundation aimed at encouraging
and supporting young adults to pursue careers in the trades. Initially envisioned
as a scholarship program to help cover the costs of attending trade schools, we
very quickly realized that there was a significant lack of interest among young
students in pursuing trade education and careers. A stigma had developed
around trade schools, making them a last resort for many talented young people.
As we are all aware, our state and nation urgently need more skilled individuals in the trades to address our mounting infrastructure needs. Tradespeople
earn good wages and they play a crucial part in enhancing our quality of life.
Therefore, we decided to pivot our program’s focus toward breaking down
these barriers, eliminating the stigma associated with working in the trades,
and attracting more students to these valuable and crucial careers.
This year we launched a program aptly named “Working Tools” in the San
Diego area which is set to reach thousands of high school students with the goal
of making the trades appealing and popular. Hundreds of enthusiastic students
will receive training in various trades, including the automotive industry and
infrastructure maintenance. On October 8, this program was officially launched
at the automotive shop of Madison High School in San Diego, making it possible
for their students to be provided with the best faculty and training possible.
We will eventually extend the program by providing additional funding at high
schools and in other trade areas up and down the state. I extend my heartfelt and
very sincere thanks to the California Masonic Foundation for their unwavering
support and collaboration in developing the Working Tools program which has
the potential to make a significant positive impact on the lives of young adults
and the state.
Appreciation
Serving as grand master of the Grand Lodge of California has been one of the
greatest honors of my life. Together, we have achieved significant milestones

Respectfully submitted,

Randall L. Brill, Grand Master

REPORT OF THE
DEPUTY GRAND MASTER
2023-2024 GRAND LODGE BUDGET

Dear brethren,
I would like to express my gratitude to the masters, wardens, and
esteemed members of the grand lodge for their unwavering support and confidence in entrusting me with the vital responsibility of crafting the budget for
the upcoming fiscal year.
During the previous Annual Communication, the brethren wholeheartedly
endorsed the per capita proposal, and this budget is a testament to our collective
efforts in utilizing that per capita and other revenue sources to further the cause
and progress of our beloved fraternity. With that, I present this budget proposal,
covering the period from November 1, 2023 through October 31, 2024. This
proposal is designed to sustain our vital programs and services while aligning
with the strategic priorities outlined in our 2025 Fraternity Plan.
Membership plays a pivotal role in our budgetary considerations. As previously discussed, we experienced a decline of just over 4,000 members due to
our temporary inability to accept applications and confer degrees in 2020–2021.
Over the past two years, our lodges have diligently worked to rectify this situation by bringing those who patiently waited into full membership. Despite still
facing challenges in the form of suspensions due to non-payment of dues, we
have managed to lay a strong foundation that allows us to plan for the future.
Thankfully, prudent financial management during the pandemic has resulted
in surplus reserves, which we are now utilizing to bridge the gap. By maintaining our commitment to meeting the significant interest in membership and
enhancing our efforts in member retention, we position ourselves favorably to
meet our financial obligations. Together, our continued focus and dedication
will ensure the financial stability and growth of our fraternity.
Our total budgeted revenue stands at slightly over $4.5 million, with
$264,000 drawn from our operating reserve to meet our financial needs. Notably,
income from per capita amounts to $2.15 million, representing a modest increase
of 1.7% compared to the previous year. Additionally, our revenue sources encompass a dividend of $435,000 from the Nob Hill Masonic Center; a generous

72

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

grant of $285,000 from the California Masonic Foundation earmarked for supporting leadership and education programs; $345,000 in reimbursement from
investments, services, and background check fees; and an additional $187,000
in revenue from other sources. This financial framework will enable us to effectively fund our vital initiatives and continue advancing our fraternity’s mission.
Financial challenges we’re addressing in this budget include increased
property insurance and health insurance premiums. These increases are affecting every industry in this state, and we are no exception. Total expenses equal
revenue in this budget, with just a small projected surplus of $8,000.
The important programs and services that are funded by this budget include:

In addition, this budget also establishes a Masonic building improvement
fund in recognition of the escalating property insurance rates in California,
accompanied by rising premiums and deductibles. As many of our buildings
require upgrades to meet new insurance standards, we aim to address this
need by introducing a grant program. These grants will assist lodges and halls
in executing necessary repairs and enhancements to their facilities. Allocation
of grants will be contingent on various factors, including the scope of the
improvement plan, historical significance, lodge membership, financial capacity,
and insurability. To fund this initiative, the budget earmarks
$300,000 from the existing reserve designated for new lodge development,
effectively reallocating these resources for this purpose upon your adoption of
the budget.
I want to express my sincere gratitude for the outstanding efforts of our
grand treasurer, grand secretary, the dedicated finance staff, and our esteemed
finance committee members in collaboratively shaping this budget. Additionally,
I extend my appreciation to the masters, wardens, and all those who attended
our spring leadership retreats for providing valuable feedback on this budget.
Brethren, your unwavering support in adopting the per capita proposal
last year was instrumental. As we look ahead to our 2025 plan, which holds
the promise of a remarkable future for our fraternity, I humbly request your
participation in the adoption of this budget. Let’s come together to shine the
light of Freemasonry upon the world.

• Professional public relations and communications efforts to create
positive awareness of Masonry, to encourage Masons to discuss
Masonry with their family and friends, and to continue promoting the
fraternity and earning media for our good work.
• Financial services to lodges and halls including accounting services, dues collection, tax return services, and tax-exempt status
restoration.
• Real estate and insurance services and support for lodges and halls.
• Leadership training events including the Master and Warden Retreats,
Secretary and Treasurer Retreats, Inspector Retreats, and the Lodge
Management Certification Program.
• Membership development efforts connecting thousands of prospects
to our lodges and providing valuable resources like the Simple Guide to
Freemasonry.
• New lodge development efforts, which so far have created more than
30 new lodges in the state.
• Masonic education, including support for programs like the
International Conference on Freemasonry, the annual California
Masonic Symposium, and the Candidate Learning Center.
• Membership management through iMember, a Grand View product
now used by three-quarters of U.S. grand lodges.
• Ritual education and training including ritual conferences and the
annual ritual competition.
• Communications to Masons, widows, and the general public through
various platforms such as California Freemason magazine, the monthly
electronic newsletter The Leader, all-member emails, and engagement
with audiences through social media channels. This includes the
creation of new video content and the maintenance of more than 145
lodge and hall websites.

Respectfully submitted,

G. Sean Metroka, Deputy Grand Master

(10,881,767) $

The Grand Lodge has several sources of income. Historically, the primary revenue sources have been Per
Capita and degree fees. The Grand Lodge Endowment Fund was created in 1992 and generates income
from the investment returns. To better manage the income from the Endowment, a 4.5% spending policy has been
instituted, calculated on a rolling five-year market value average to protect the fund principle. The Grand Lodge has other
finance income, such as investment and interest income. The Grand Lodge receives dues from the Grand Master’s Lodge.
In 2004, the California Masonic Foundation included in its mission the funding of Masonic education and leadership
training programs and now provides a grant for such purposes. In 2005, the delegates of the 156th Annual
Communication adopted a $30 application fee to be paid to Grand Lodge by all applicants for the degrees of Masonry
and out-of-state affiliations. The Grand Lodge provides services throughout the state and receives reimbursement for
certain expenses incurred from the Masonic Services Bureaus funds. The Grand Lodge manages the investments of its
related entities and receives reimbursement equal to the cost of providing those services. The Grand Lodge is the sole
shareholder of the Nob Hill Masonic Center Inc. and receives dividends on the profits of this Corporation. The Grand
Lodge also receives support from reserves generated from prior fiscal years' surplus/operating reserves to balance its
budget.
