GRAND MASTER’S
INSTALLATION ADDRESS
Thank you all for joining us here today.
I am humbled to stand before you, having now been entrusted with
the leadership and welfare of our ancient and honorable fraternity in this
jurisdiction.
Thinking back on the path I have travelled to this place, on this day, I most
certainly did not imagine that this responsibility might be in my future—in fact
nothing of the sort. I was quite happy in retirement and contentedly enjoying
life when “that call” arrived. Nevertheless, I am grateful and freely acknowledge that this is a wonderful and life-changing calling and one to which I am
completely devoted.
I’m indebted to so many people who have helped to make it possible for
an awkward boy from Paradise, California, to develop into someone others
might think worthy of such an honor and awesome trust. I am convinced that
my journey began with the mentorship and excellent examples provided by
Master Masons in my youth. My father was a Mason and he insisted that I join
the Order of DeMolay when I became old enough. I recall the transformational
effect Masonry had on my father, though I didn’t really understand it at the time.
The Masons who served as advisors during my active service in DeMolay
positively changed the direction of my life. Masons like Don Henderson, Mike
Scroggins, Ed Faulkenstein, Milton Kite, Paul Dawson, Floyd Prather, and Dr.
Richard Murrill. These men, along with so many others, were the adults I called
“Dad” who mentored me and taught me the value of service and, each in their
own way, the importance of Freemasonry, and who, by their examples, taught
us to follow in their footsteps on the path of good and upright living.
Our theme this year is simply “Share the Light of Freemasonry.” I intend
this theme to be a call for action by all California Masons.
Many of you know that I served for more than 30 years in the United States
Marine Corps. My service took me to many different countries and regularly
afforded me the enlightening opportunity to get to know people whose circumstances were vastly different than my own. What most surprised me about
these experiences was the revelation that we are very similar to one another in
our essential hopes and aspirations in life and that our differences are trivial
in comparison. At a basic level, we all want liberty and happiness. We want our

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

83

children to have a good education and to have at least as good a life as we have.
We want to have an honorable means of supporting ourselves and our families,
and we want to be useful. We want a reasonable measure of security and to live
in peace and harmony with our fellow man. I mention this here because it has
occurred to me that as Masons we are particularly well-equipped to achieve
these goals and to help others do the same.
We all understand that there is a direct connection between education
and freedom. Masons have been directly promoting education, freedom, and
basic rights for all regardless of origin, race, religion, wealth, or gender for most
of this country’s history. It might interest you to know that many California
Masons have led this charge in our nation. A California Mason wrote the 15th
Amendment to the U.S. Constitution guaranteeing the right to vote without
regard to race, color, or previous condition of servitude. Another California
Mason wrote the 29 words that would later become the 19th Amendment, guaranteeing women the right to vote. And still another led the U.S. Supreme Court
in decisions which ushered in the end of racial segregation in schools, protected
interracial marriage, and established the constitutional rights advisement or
“Miranda marning” requirement in our criminal justice system.
When I selected “Share the Light of Freemasonry” as a theme, I didn’t
realize how often the idea had been promoted by those who have come before
me. After reading the installation addresses of California grand masters who
have served during the last 30 years, I learned that most of them promoted this
action in one way or another. This truly is not a new idea, but it is an important
one. What we have as Masons is a tremendous benefit to humanity and should
be shared and expanded.
I recently read an article published in 1924 in which the author described
Masonry as “a serious undertaking” and that it “exists to make men wiser and
happier. It is a great force for good—a force that binds, into one universal brotherhood, men who believe in the power of moral principals… Masonry is a body of
good people bound by ties of fraternity, working for the common good and for
the preservation of moral truths, unhampered by bigotry or blind intolerance.”
Our principal tenets of brotherly love, relief, and truth are not just a slogan
that helps us to feel good about ourselves. They are a way of life for good people
everywhere.
With this understanding, it should be easy to see why the whole of humanity is improved when more people intentionally follow moral principles such
as those taught in our fraternity. In short, I believe our world will be greatly
improved when we welcome more good people into Freemasonry.
In support of this overarching theme and in consideration of the current
needs of our jurisdiction, I have established a few objectives.
To continue our work toward full implementation of our 2025 Fraternity
Plan and the pillars of true friendship, diversity and harmony, and positive awareness. We will also begin the process of developing our successor strategic plan.
To strengthen member retention efforts in our lodges by streamlining locator

84

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

services to reconnect with our brothers who have lost touch with their lodge,
enhancing the member restoration program, and by establishing a suspension-prevention program which will strengthen our efforts to restore to good standing
members who have become at risk of suspension.
To increase our active support of Masonic youth orders by engaging more
Masons in the service of our chapters, bethels, and assemblies and by developing an internal program for identifying and recruiting Masons as mentors and
advisors for our youth. We must find our way back to the program of Masons
personally showing up for our youth, rather than simply giving them funding
and a place to meet.
To engage and support military veterans in California. Veterans serving in
conflicts most often experience a deep sense of camaraderie while performing
selfless service for their countrymen. When they leave their uniforms behind,
a great sense of loss may follow. In Freemasonry, veterans commonly find
something that fills, at least partially, that void. We owe a great debt to the men
and women who have faithfully served our country in uniform. There are many
ways to show our appreciation of their sacrifices and I am asking our lodges
and members to connect with veterans’ organizations in their communities to
provide help where it is needed.
To continue to support our California Masonic Foundation and its programs,
as well as local organizations serving the communities in which our lodges
reside. The need for support in elder care, early childhood education and literacy
programs, and of our distressed worthy brothers seem to be ever increasing, and
I’m confident we will meet them, as we always have.
To strengthen our relationships with the Most Worshipful Prince Hall
Grand Lodge of California and the Grand Lodge of Iran (In Exile) and develop
a more supportive relationship with other worthy Masonic traditions practicing in the State of California. I believe that we can work together to provide a
greater benefit to humanity without risking our own traditions or violating our
various constitutions.
Lastly, I’m calling on all our Masonic family to foster harmony in every part
of our lives. This necessarily begins in our lodges. We know that disharmony has
a way of creeping into the most well-intentioned gatherings of human beings.
Nevertheless, Masons are very well equipped to assist in the resolution of conflict, promote acceptance and understanding, and to teach others to do the same.
It is my fervent hope that you will join me in achieving these objectives as
we share the light of Freemasonry together.
The many good people who assisted me through my formative years and
helped me overcome the challenges of life are certainly too numerous to list
here. However, I am most grateful to my wife, Margaret. Next month we will
celebrate our 40th wedding anniversary. When we met, I was already a Mason
and an officer of the Marines. She likely didn’t understand what she was in for
with me, but she quickly learned, and she didn’t run away, as other reasonable
people might have. Instead, she has helped me focus on the good when I became

mired in the bad; has been a stabilizing force when I felt my foundation falter;
and encouraged me to not let this opportunity pass me by, because she knew I
would forever struggle with the resulting feeling of regret. I love you, Margaret,
and I am a much better person walking beside you on the road of life. Thank you!
Respectfully submitted,

G. Sean Metroka, Grand Master

REPORT OF THE
SENIOR GRAND WARDEN
2024–2025 PER CAPITA PROPOSAL
Arthur L. Salazar Jr., Senior Grand Warden

Dear Brethren,
As senior grand warden, it is my duty to present to you the per capita proposal which will fund the grand lodge budget during the fiscal year of November
1, 2024, through October 31, 2025. This per capita will be collected next summer
based on the number of Masons on the rolls of each lodge on June 30, 2024.
As the deputy grand master shared, we are still recovering from the COVID19 pandemic, but our opportunities for growth and success are greater than
our challenges. We know that there is significant interest in membership in
Freemasonry. The thousands of prospects who have sought us out are proof
that Freemasonry is not only relevant and respected but greatly needed in our
communities today. In drafting a budget for the 175th year of our grand lodge, I
have relied upon the best available data on membership trends and various financial indicators to anticipate the trajectory of our challenges and opportunities.
Through your efforts in working with prospects to become friends and then
brothers, I am optimistic that our membership will stabilize and could even
grow over the next few years. This will help offset the impact of post-pandemic
inflation across goods and services that all organizations must now face. In
fiscal year 2025, we have significantly decreased the reliance on the distribution
from previous surpluses as those reserves are nearly depleted. Overall, our plan
accounts for inflation of 5 percent in fraternal and administrative expenses,
while keeping appropriations at a modest 2 percent increase. As a result of
this inflation, coupled with the decrease in revenue, prudence requires that I
propose a $5.00 increase in per capita.
Therefore, the per capita I propose for the fiscal year 2025 is $65.50.
As a past grand treasurer and a CPA, I am confident that this plan will
serve the best interests of the fraternity. With your support of this proposal,
we will be able to continue delivering to our lodges those important programs
and services they have requested, such as leadership training and education,

90

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

communications, technology, financial and administrative services, and the
initiatives to increase positive public awareness and membership growth.
Working together, I am confident that we can continue to create more
positive awareness of our fraternity, continue to improve the organization, and
grow our membership so that all of our lodges may prosper and each one of
you may inspire those around you to create a world in harmony. I look forward
to being on this journey with you!
Thank you for your support!

REPORT OF THE
GRAND TREASURER
Most Worshipful Grand Master and Brethren all,
Serving as your grand treasurer for the second term, I am pleased
to report on the financial health of our grand lodge and its related entities. We
continue to benefit from the efforts and expertise of our brethren who volunteer
their time as board members and committee members, including our entire
grand lodge financial services team led by Carol Hunter, our CFO; Maribel
Pasamic, our controller; Khalil Sweidy, our director of financial planning and
real estate; and of course Very Worshipful Allan Casalou, our grand secretary.
The audit committee, led by Worshipful Tony Garcia, continues to work
closely with Moss Adams, as our outside auditor, and ensures that our financial
statement audits for all our grand lodge entities continue to go smoothly. As
of our last fiscal year ending October 31, 2022, each of our entities once again
received a clean audit opinion and were informed that our internal controls
remain effective and that our model for shared service costs is not only appropriate but consistent with best practices and within industry standards.
The finance committee, led by Worshipful Levon Keshishian, continues to
bring its vast corporate experience to our budgeting process in working with
our deputy grand master and senior grand warden to provide wise and timely
counsel in the preparation of their annual budgets and per capita calculations.
The members of the insurance committee, led by Worshipful David M.
Anderson, continues their untiring work in their detailed review of our vast
and complex insurance needs not only for our grand lodge entities but also
for our lodges and hall associations. They have this year moved our complex
insurance needs to a new provider. This includes an ongoing review of claims
to ensure a premier result for the benefit of the craft and to find ways to deliver
its services in the most cost-efficient method possible.
The investments committee, led by Worshipful Wil Smith, is deeply
immersed in ongoing efforts to monitor the economic factors which impact
our portfolio. In their ongoing evaluation of our investment policies, they
continue to recommend that 4.5 percent of our investment portfolio be distributed to fund the Grand Lodge operating budget, aligned to preserve and
grow our overall portfolio for future use. The relationship with NEPC as our
investment advisory firm, which began six years ago, continues to bring forth

best) Masonic jurisdictions in the world. It is an honor to be a California Mason.

While our master trust has gained a respectable size, we all must remember
that these funds are not available to simply withdraw to cover the expense needs
of the several entities. For best practices, we are limited to draw 4.5 percent
and up to 4.75 percent of the 20-quarter average of the investments for each
entity to support their operations. What this means that in the example of the
Masonic Homes, with a current operating budget of approximately $70 million
and an investment distribution of approximately $41 million, we have a delta of
approximately $29 million that needs to be made up from other sources such
as fees for certain services and each of our annual contributions in fulfillment
of our ongoing obligations to each other.
In 1992, our grand lodge created an endowment funded each year by the
budget surplus of each grand master. Since that time, the endowment fund
has grown to $2.8 million as of July 31, 2023 from $2.7 million in July 31, 2022.
This allowed us to normalize our budgets and per capita assessments, specifically during the economic impact of COVID-19 on our operations at Nob Hill
Masonic Center and the California Masonic Memorial Temple. We have accrued
these actual surpluses as deferred assets for our operating reserves. This same
endowment fund will now provide $263,841 for the budget of Right Worshipful

REPORT OF THE
GRAND SECRETARY
Most Worshipful Grand Master and members of the grand lodge,
I am pleased to present this, my 16th report as your grand secretary.

Membership Information
Current Membership Statistics
As of June 30, 2023, we had 39,051 active Masons, including 2,535 Entered
Apprentices and nine Fellow Crafts. Our Masonic family also includes 12,320
widows. Please refer to my written report for detailed membership activity,
by-law amendments, life memberships, and veterans’ awards.
While initiations and other degree conferrals decreased 9 percent from
2022 when we had pent-up degree demand from the pandemic closure, our
2023 membership year showed resilience and reflects positively on the future.
The number of applications received in 2023 was the most since 2016. Lodges
conferred as many degrees as we did before the pandemic. Most notably, suspensions for nonpayment of dues decreased by nearly 20 percent.
As we look to the next year, three membership initiatives underscore
our path to a vibrant future: prospect engagement, member retention, and
restoration.
Prospect Engagement
In fiscal year 2023, we received inquiries from more than 5,000 qualified prospects statewide. As highlighted in the grand master’s report, a significant milestone was achieved when more than half of our lodges actively engaged with
these prospects, resulting in many lodges successfully welcoming new members
into our fraternity. However, it’s important to acknowledge that approximately
45 percent of our lodges missed the opportunity to connect with the prospects
assigned to them, leaving around 2,400 prospects uncontacted.
The encouraging aspect of this situation is the evident and robust interest
in becoming a part of Freemasonry. The key to our immediate future lies in the
collective effort of all our lodges to engage these interested men effectively.

114

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

To facilitate this crucial engagement, we introduced the role of a lodge prospect
manager in the past year. I am pleased to report that nearly 100 lodges have
appointed a dedicated brother to fulfill this role. We have conducted online
workshops with these prospect managers, providing them with valuable insights,
best practices, and efficient processes within the prospect system. This initiative
aims to enhance the effectiveness of our engagement strategies and ensure a
seamless onboarding experience for new members.
Looking ahead to 2024, it is our fervent hope that every lodge will identify
and appoint a prospect manager within their ranks. These individuals play a
pivotal role in strengthening our fraternity by bridging the gap between interested prospects and our lodges. For those lodges that have not yet designated
a prospect manager, I urge you to prioritize this appointment before the year’s
end. By embracing this vital role, we can collectively harness the existing interest
in Freemasonry, welcoming new members with open arms and ensuring the
continued growth and vitality of our beloved institution.

Member Restoration

Member Retention
Making a Mason demands significant dedication from both the individual Mason
and his lodge. Initiating, passing, and raising new brothers require substantial
time and effort. Reflecting on the hours we invest in these processes underscores the importance of member retention. Effective communication, engaging
lodge programs, and streamlined dues collection processes are key to member
retention and pivotal in ensuring our fraternity’s strength.
This year, our efforts in dues collection resulted in a notable decrease in
suspensions. Building on this success, we aim to enhance the member experience by further simplifying the dues payment process. As an illustration, I am a
member of three lodges. With the centralized dues billing system implemented
a few years ago, I can effortlessly pay my dues to all three lodges in a single
transaction on my phone, taking less than two minutes. This convenience has
been embraced by an increasing number of our members.
Looking ahead, we plan to introduce a new feature allowing periodic recurring dues. With this enhancement, members can proactively pay their 2024
dues and set up recurring payments for their 2025 dues, whether on a monthly,
quarterly, or annual basis, with the full amount settled by the end of 2024. This
innovation ensures timely payments, thereby reducing the risk of suspension.
By expanding the pool of members in good standing, we strengthen our lodges
and fortify our fraternity.
Currently, over 75 percent of our lodges actively participate in the centralized dues billing service, which continues to evolve and improve. These lodges
demonstrate higher dues collection rates and fewer member suspensions on
average compared to non-participating lodges. If your lodge is part of the
remaining 25 percent that has not yet embraced this system, joining the majority
could significantly enhance your member retention.

115

Over the past five years, we have suspended nearly 6,000 members for non-payment of dues. Our surveys have revealed that a considerable number of these
brothers lost touch with their lodges but expressed a genuine desire to be
reinstated.
In response to this issue, we focused on the restoration program during
the spring and summer months, which yielded promising results. A total of 340
members were successfully restored across 167 participating lodges. What’s
particularly noteworthy is that lodges involved in the program restored twice as
many members on average compared to those not participating. If this success
had been replicated across all our lodges, we could have potentially reduced
our membership loss by a third, solely through this initiative.
The restoration program was initially introduced in 2019, and since then,
more than 2,000 members have been reinstated. Analyzing four years of data,
we’ve observed that members restored through this program tend to continue
their dues payments in subsequent years. Only a small fraction find themselves
in arrears again, indicating the long-term effectiveness of this approach.
It is our collective responsibility to the future of our fraternity to actively
engage with our suspended members. By working closely with those who express
a willingness to be restored, we can bring them back into our fold, not only bolstering our numbers but also strengthening the very fabric of our fraternity. This
proactive outreach is not just about reinstating members; it’s about reaffirming
our commitment to each other and the future of Freemasonry.

New Lodge Development
Our focus on new lodge development remains steadfast and productive. Since
the launch of this initiative in 2016, we have successfully instituted 38 new
lodges, including three this year. Four more are in the pipeline. Tomorrow, a
comprehensive report on charters will be presented, but let me emphasize that
expanding the number of lodges statewide is pivotal for our future sustainability.
Due to the pandemic challenges, nearly two dozen lodges have contemplated
consolidation due to a shortage of willing officers and hall association pressures.
Overcoming these hurdles is undoubtedly complex, yet our dedicated efforts are
geared toward finding solutions that offer better outcomes compared to mere
lodge mergers, which often result in losing a valuable community presence.
We are committed to preserving our footprint in every community we serve
and to reaching new communities where Freemasonry does not currently exist.

116

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

Positive Awareness

Financial Services

The foundation of our 2025 Fraternity Plan revolves around enhancing the positive perception of Freemasonry in California. Market research has illuminated
that people primarily seek information about Freemasonry through personal
connections, often involving family members, friends, or mentors who are or
were Masons. However, a significant number of Masons do not discuss the fraternity with their close circles due to various reasons, ranging from perceived
restrictions to personal discomfort. To address this challenge, we have diligently
pursued three key initiatives this year.
First, we launched the #ImAMason campaign urging our members to
share their Masonic journeys online using the hashtag #ImAMason. The campaign, which ran for two weeks on Facebook and Instagram from July 10, 2023,
exceeded our expectations. While our goal was to reach 3 million impressions
and 300 posts, the campaign generated over 700 posts, reaching an impressive
6 million viewers. Notably, grand lodges from other parts of the world joined
us and inspired a Spanish version, #SoyMason, which was enthusiastically
embraced by the Grand Lodge of Baja California and other Spanish-speaking
jurisdictions.
Secondly, we continued to distribute substantial quantities of A Simple
Guide to Masonry, equipping every brother with valuable insights into some of
the most intricate topics in Masonry, including gender, religion, and secrecy.
This guide serves as a comprehensive resource for both Masons and non-Masons, fostering informed conversations about Masonry. Keeping a copy handy
proves instrumental in improving one’s ability to discuss Masonry confidently.
Engaging in conversations about Masonry is not only enjoyable but also
crucial for creating awareness and interest in our fraternity. This brings us to
our third initiative—a paid positive awareness campaign. Over a span of 10
weeks, from August 15 to October 31, we conducted a strategic social media
ad campaign promoting Freemasonry in California. In the initial eight weeks
alone, the campaign delivered hundreds of thousands of ads and elicited 1,452
requests for information about membership.

Programs And Services
The focus of the grand lodge office is to provide quality services and programs,
which reduce administrative burdens and prioritize the member experience.
Member Services
Our Member Services team provides core support to lodges and members. Over
the past year, they processed more than 14,000 information and service requests,
a 20 percent increase from last year, completing more than 90 percent on the
first day with an average completion time of 150 minutes.

117

The Financial Services team provides accounting, budgeting, reporting, and
audit support for the grand lodge and our related entities. Additionally, they
provide a variety of supportive programs and resources for lodges and halls.
Today, nearly 82 percent of lodges and 60 percent of halls are using Intacct
as their accounting solution and are receiving high quality service from the grand
lodge finance team. This year, Financial Services prepared and filed over 500
tax returns for lodges, hall associations, and residents of the Masonic Homes.
Real Estate Services
Our dedicated real estate services team continues to provide comprehensive
property-related support to our lodges and halls. Addressing the complexities
of managing a lodge, the team offers daily guidance via calls and emails, aiding
lodges in navigating the intricate aspects of property management. In addition
to maintaining several grand lodge-owned properties, this year, the team played
a pivotal role in facilitating the acquisition of the Masonic Hall in Sonora.
Recognizing Sonora as a community where preserving a Masonic presence is crucial, efforts are underway to attract commercial tenants and enhance the lodge
space, aiming to reinvigorate Freemasonry in this historically significant town.
It is imperative for every lodge with a hall to critically assess the condition of their building. The challenging landscape of property insurance in
California, exacerbated by persistent wildfires, has led to escalating premiums
and deductibles, making it increasingly challenging to sustain and operate our
halls. Insurance carriers now require higher valuations to align with current
market conditions and demand improvements to fortify aging structures. In
response, it is essential for us to explore strategic solutions and consider all
available options. Together, we must enhance our buildings to meet these
evolving standards, ensuring the enduring presence and vitality of our Masonic
meeting places.
Communications
Our communications team brilliantly executes a comprehensive strategy for
our fraternity, employing a multifaceted approach that includes various websites, social media platforms, targeted email campaigns, a monthly leadership
e-newsletter, and our esteemed California Freemason magazine, which has once
again garnered prestigious national accolades in the publishing industry.
The team has created of high-quality video content, enriching our social
media, website, and other communication channels. Their efforts extend beyond
the grand lodge and its entities, as they have developed and maintain websites
for over 150 lodges and 60 halls, fostering a robust online presence for our
Masonic community.
This year, our communications initiatives have been recognized with six
awards from the Association of Media and Publishing. Notable accolades include

118

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

a silver award for the compelling video showcasing Panamericana Lodge, another
silver award for the best blog post recounting the 1909 tour to Mexico titled
“The Travelling Trowel Train,” and a silver award for the best single-topic magazine issue, highlighting Masonry in Central and South America under the title
“Southern Exposure.” To top it off, our magazine earned three prestigious gold
awards for design excellence and general excellence, solidifying our position
with two of the industry’s top honors. These accomplishments underscore our
team’s unwavering commitment to excellence and innovation in communicating
the essence of Freemasonry to our members and beyond.

Appreciation

Recognition Of Foreign Grand Lodges
It is my responsibility to inform the grand master of matters pertaining to
foreign grand lodge recognition and to present to you, in the form of a motion,
the recognition of certain grand lodges that meet our criteria. The grand lodge
has received the following requests for recognition by foreign grand lodges:
Brazil: In Brazil, there is a national grand orient, a separate confederation
of 27 state grand lodges, and independent state grand orients, which are separate and sovereign from the national grand orient. Our grand lodge currently
recognizes the Grand Orient of Brazil, all 27 state grand lodges, and several of
the independent state grand orients. We have received a request for mutual
recognition from two of the independent state grand orients.
Grand Orient of Bahia: The Independent Grand Orient of Bahai was
founded on January 29, 1990. This grand lodge is a member of the Brazilian
Masonic Confederation and the Inter-American Masonic Confederation. It
enjoys mutual recognition with the two other grand lodges in the same territory
whom we recognize.
Grand Orient of Minas Gerais: This grand lodge was founded on
September 12, 1944. It worked under the national Grand Orient of Brazil until
1973. This grand lodge is a member of the Brazilian Masonic Confederation and
the Inter-American Masonic Confederation. It enjoys mutual recognition with
the two other grand lodges in the same territory whom we recognize.
The Commission on Information for Recognition confirms that these grand
lodges meet the recognition standards of the Conference of Grand Master
of Masons of North America and we find that they meet the requirements in
California.
Therefore, I move that the Grand Lodge of California enter into agreements
of mutual recognition with the Grand Orient of Bahia and the Grand Orient
of Minas Gerais.

119

In concluding my report, I extend my heartfelt gratitude to the lodge secretaries
and assistant secretaries, whose unwavering dedication forms the backbone
of our jurisdiction. I also express my thanks to our assistant grand lecturers
and district inspectors, whose ritual duties are complemented by invaluable
administrative support throughout the year.
I have had the honor of working alongside Very Worshipful Brother Charles
Cross, our grand treasurer, who has diligently served his second term. Our grand
lecturer, Very Worshipful Brother Ricky Lawler, has continued his dedicated
service as the custodian of the ritual. I rely a great deal on their leadership in
their respective roles and I enjoy our teamwork and friendship.
My sincere appreciation goes to the skilled professionals in our grand
lodge office, individuals deeply passionate about our fraternity, whose dedicated service upholds our mission. I commend them all for their unwavering
commitment and excellent work.
Lastly, I want to express my gratitude to our grand master, Most Worshipful
Brother Randy Brill. He demonstrated the very essence of perseverance, managing a very busy schedule and addressing several challenges along the way. He
championed the remarkable efforts of our lodges and fostered closer connections with other grand lodges in California and Mexico. Most Worshipful, thank
you for your outstanding service and for your genuine friendship.
And thank you, my brothers, for the opportunity to serve and work with you.
Respectfully submitted,
Allan L. Casalou, Grand Secretary

REPORT OF THE
GRAND LECTURER
Most Worshipful Grand Master, grand lodge officers, members of grand lodge,
and brethren all,
This is my fifth report to you, my brethren, as your grand lecturer. At our
ritual committee meetings in November and December, we outlined the goals
and tasks we wanted to accomplish for this year.
I again asked for and received copies of the calendars from each of our
district inspectors to ensure that the proper information was reaching our
lodge officers to assist them in their planning efforts. The work in the third
degree was exemplified in our division Master Mason seminars for divisions I,
III, V, VII and IX.
Projects this year included a consolidation of instructions pertinent to
our constituent lodge installation ceremony, an update to the “Music in our
Lodges” letter and inspectors’ manual, and a translation of our lodge constitution ceremony into Spanish.
We have completed work on seven officers’ coach modules intended for
individual coursework available online for lodge leaders who have been identified
by their district inspectors as having the necessary attributes to be considered
for further training as a lodge officers’ coach.
Additionally, our 2023 ritual competition consisted of the work of the
examiner and candidate in all three degree proficiencies.

Master Mason Seminars
Master Mason seminars serve as the schools of instruction for the grand lecturer,
with the work being exemplified by the brethren of the division. Based on my
observations from the previous year, I requested that assistant grand lecturers
make arrangements to have members in their divisions work to exemplify the
third degree.
The Division III seminar was held at Martinez Lodge No. 41 on April 1;
Division VII at Arcadia Lodge No. 278 on June 17; Division IX at Orange Grove
Lodge No. 293 on July 1; Division V at Bakersfield Lodge No. 224 on August 26,
and Division I at Francis Drake Lodge No. 376 on September 9.

A Recipe For Good Ritual
In my visits to lodges and district schools of instruction, I am constantly on
the lookout for good ritual. Occasionally, I see ritual that is not performed to
our high standards, but not this year. I have been impressed by the brethren I
have visited and spoken with, who are on the right track regarding the quality
of their work and willingness to take that next step. What will that look like?
Those of you here who have had that conversation with me know who you are.
What is that next step? I look forward to the opportunity to return to your

140

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

141

lodges and districts to see what that answer is and what commitment you have
decided to make.
There is a class of brethren who are more than proficient in ritual work, but
something is missing. They obviously have memorized their work flawlessly, but
during the degree or when they speak to their brethren, something is not there…
I have observed many of our brothers performing our ritual with all the
necessary ingredients to make an excellent degree.
It takes memorization, practice with your brethren, and one other ingredient: brotherly love. My mentor, Wally Partridge, insisted that Masonic charity
or brotherly love was the essential ingredient to presenting our ritual to the
candidate. You can be great at memorization and awesome in your delivery,
but it is nothing without the charity of the ritualist to back it up. When you
sacrifice time and energy to learn our ritual and present it to the candidate in a
meaningful manner as if talking to a friend, Wally would call that true Masonic
charity. Even our own second degree perambulation, taken from 1 Corinthians,
Chapter 13, explains at the beginning... “Though I speak in the tongues of men
and of Angels and have not charity... I am only a resounding gong or clanging
cymbal…”
When you make the commitment to practice and deliver our ritual to candidates, please do not forget that essential element of brotherly love.
I was listening to the radio one day and heard a story of a young mother
who happened to be watching her son play in the front yard with another little
boy whose family had just moved to the neighborhood. The mother noticed that
the little boy who just moved in did not have many toys of his own. When her
son came back into the house, she asked him if he noticed that his new friend
didn’t have any Hot Wheels. She reminded her son that he was blessed to have
a large number of cars in his collection and made a deal with him to pick out
some cars that he might give to the neighbor boy, and for each car he picked
out, she would give him one jellybean. She stipulated that the cars he chose to
give must be his best cars, without chipped paint and with all four wheels still
attached. Her son cheerfully agreed and immediately began selecting the cars
he was going to give, which was answered by his mother stacking the jellybeans
on the counter. After her son recovered from his sugar high, the two walked to
the neighbor’s house to deliver the cars.
The ritual is the vehicle that delivers our tenets, virtues, and teachings to
the candidate. It helps draw attention to the need to be charitable to our fellow
man with our time, talent, and our treasure. Without charity or brotherly love,
the opportunity is lost. Those of us blessed to be part of another man’s degree
conferral need to identify the needs of the candidate and look within ourselves
to ask what we have to offer him in a ritual experience, free of chipped paint
and with all four wheels still attached.
Speaking of all four wheels, our ritual competition for 2023 was originally
intended to be a team effort as it had been a few years ago. The candidate’s proficiencies are a very important part of the ritual and must remain a team effort

to foster the unique relationship that must be allowed to develop between a
candidate and his mentor or coach. When the competition registration opened,
the assistant grand lecturers and I started to receive requests from individual
brothers wishing to participate in the competition by themselves. We informed
them that the work for an individual competing would consist of both the
examiner’s and candidates’ work. There was a total value of 5,926 points. In
comparison, the staircase lecture competition from seven years ago had a
combined word and floorwork total of only 1,005 points.

MESSAGE FROM THE
GRAND CHAPLAIN
What is the most common question that you as a Freemason hear? It
probably sounds something like “What do Freemasons do?” The usual responses
are that we support those in need, that we try to make the world a better place,
or the familiar “We make good men better.” But that’s what we try to do—the
result of what we do—not what Masons actually do. In truth, Masons build,
and the way we accomplish that is we plan. The most important lesson we learn
in Masonry is that a life well-lived requires a plan, a trestleboard on which we
have sketched a path. The universal symbol of our fraternity has this lesson
built right in. Not the square—that’s the functional tool we use to determine
what fits our plan. It is the compass that embodies our plan.
Most of the world is familiar with the moral compass. It’s one of the many
Masonic phrases that have entered common parlance, meaning that innate sense
of what is right and what is wrong. Note that the moral compass is not a cardinal
compass. It does not point in the general direction of right or express degrees
of wrong. That is because rightness and wrongness and mutually exclusive,
and the distinction is entirely binary. Masonry recognizes no gray area here.
We all understand that someone may see an unattended basket of apples and
evaluate the risk of taking one, the insignificant harm to the absent seller, their
own hunger and need, the hazards of being caught, and justify taking one, but
their moral compass still tells them and us that the taking is wrong. The moral
compass does not point, it circumscribes, and we learn to use it gradually.
In the first degree, we learn that we should circumscribe our desires. Decide
what we believe to be right and wrong. Both points of the compass, though, are
beneath our functional square, because we are not yet ready to use it, though
we know its function. In the second degree, we learn of the importance of education, contemplation, and preparation—the resources necessary to develop
a plan to be ready to use our compass. One point of the compass is thus made
accessible, but not quite released to our hand. In the third degree, we learn
the consequences of living by a moral code, of fulfilling our obligations, and of
the impact our life will have on others. We learn of “memento mori,” the idea
that we should consider carefully what we will leave behind and how we will
be remembered—how we impact others. Only then is the other point raised,
the compass freed to us, for only then are we prepared to use the compass to
describe the boundaries of our conduct in life.

146

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

As a Master Mason, we use our moral compass to draw that circle around
ourselves and decide in advance what is within it (that which is right) and what
is without it (that which is wrong). In doing so, Masons distinguish themselves
by their focus on self. We are less concerned with how the conduct of others
affects us, and more with how our conduct affects others. We search for our
imperfections and work each day to be a bit better, to gradually improve our
spiritual ashlar. We test constantly with our moral square.
On a larger scale, as a fraternity, we have a plan. We pass along to others
the importance of planning and make available the tools of preparation. We
support literacy, the foundation of education. We support family, the foundation
of morality, love, and caring. We promote responsible friendship and leadership
among young people, the foundation of social bonding. We nurture academic
education and skilled training in the trades through our new Working Tools
program, preparing people to provide for themselves and their family, as well
as to contribute to the care of those less fortunate. Together we create relief
programs and of course provide for those at our Masonic Homes.
These are all important. All are most admirable, and each of you has every
reason to be proud. Congratulations!
Now, though, let us consider our shortcomings. This year we have focused
on “Fulfilling Our Obligations,” and Most Worshipful Brill has posed a question
to us all: “Does your lodge look like the community in which it exists and, if
not, why not?” He is asking whether you have an impact in your community
that inspires the citizenry to not only appreciate your lodge but to emulate
it; to want to be a part of it. The folks you see in the grocery store shop there
because it serves them. The same applies to Target and Walmart, Home Depot
and Costco, Applebee’s and Olive Garden, and also your community churches,
synagogues, and mosques. The members of the community go to those places
for good reasons. People get what they need in their lives. They know what
they’re going to find when they arrive, and those places are open. Their lights
are on, they are welcoming, and the benefits of being there are known right away.
You will not find your community members in dark places, the purpose
of which is unknown. Places where the oft-asked question “What do you do
there?” is not answered.
I want you to ask yourself an important question. Ask it as you journey
home, and really think about it. And please be honest with yourself. If your
home lodge vanished overnight—if it ceased to exist—would your community
even notice?
Would your Nextdoor app be alive with people asking where it went? Would
its loss trend on Twitter (I’m sorry, on “X”)? Or would there be an insignificant
social media ripple, one lone poster saying, “Huh. I always wondered what they
did there.”
In short, I am asking whether you and your brothers have considered the
memento mori of your lodge. Whether you—your lodge—have a place in your
community, one that your fellow citizens know about. Whether you and your

lodge are being a good citizen, one that contributes, is admired, and inspires.
Whether, as a lodge, you have fulfilled your obligations, or whether you hold
yourself separate and apart, perhaps above, those “other” people. Whether,
perhaps, your lodge needs to sit down and sketch out a plan on its trestleboard;
perhaps relearn how it uses its moral compass.
I sincerely hope that you here assembled ponder this and return home
ready to develop your lodge’s plan to be a force in your city or town—your plan
to exist in your community as a part of your community. Your plan to really
fulfill your obligations by sharing the light of Freemasonry. Share it on your
social media, share it in your world, share it by the example you set. Turn on
the lights and illuminate the “Yes, We’re Open” sign brightly, vividly, so that
your lodge becomes what it is intended to be: a beacon to illuminate life’s path
and to help those around you navigate safely. Because when you share the light
of Freemasonry, the world around you will be able to see for themselves what
Freemasons do.
Respectfully submitted,
Ralph C. Shelton II, Grand Chaplain

GRAND ORATION
October 2023

Most Worshipful Brill, most worshipful sirs, worshipful brethren, and brethren all,
Good morning. It is truly an honor to speak to you this morning, one for which
I am forever grateful. This year I had the opportunity to travel the state, and
even travel to our nation’s capital to meet new brothers and to really learn more
about what it means to be a Mason by seeing Masonry in action.
As I considered my topic for today’s oration, I wanted to find a way to share
some of what I learned representing your grand lodge throughout this year. One
of Most Worshipful Brill’s focus points was “fulfilling our obligations,” and I
had ample opportunity to witness brothers fulfilling their obligations while
travelling as grand orator. Thus, I decided that would be the basis of my talk
with you this morning. Of course, I immediately found this to be more difficult
than I had anticipated, for although I am speaking to a group of Master Masons,
my words are in writing and may be published in some form or another. This
means that in order for me to fulfill my obligation, I must be careful what I
write about this topic. Still, I think it possible for me to give you some food for
thought about fulfilling our obligations and demonstrate that, like most things
in Masonry, there’s more to it than first meets the eye.
If you are like me, when you hear the phrase “fulfilling our obligations,”
your mind immediately goes to the three obligations we took at the altar when
going through the degrees. However, if we look at the definition of obligation,
we will see that it should mean much more than that. The term is defined as
“an act or course of action to which a person is morally or legally bound; a duty
or a commitment.” By that definition we are obligated, or morally bound, to
everything introduced to us in lodge. Our formal obligations, certainly, but also
the charges, the perambulations, the lectures, the prayers, the working tools,
and everything contained in the degrees. If we accept that, we must also accept
that we are obligated to follow the constitutions, laws, rules, and edicts from
the grand lodge. With all that in mind, let’s consider some of the ways we might
think about fulfilling our obligations. Please keep in mind that it is not my intent
to tickle your ears or be a cheerleader. I hope to challenge you to think about
fulfilling your obligations in a few different or new ways.

152

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

153

Studying the first-degree perambulation, we learn that it is not for the
candidate but rather for we, the Master Masons who are officers or on the
sidelines. It clearly shows us that we are responsible for the level of brotherhood and unity in our lodges. It tells us that the younger, or newer Masons
thirst for brotherhood and unity and it is up to us to give it to them. Further,
that for the fraternity to survive, the more senior we get, the greater that
responsibility. The perambulation shows that in order for us to fulfill our
obligations, we must do everything in our power to foster brotherhood and
unity within our lodges.
In the second-degree perambulation, we are reintroduced to the tenets of
faith, hope, and charity. This is to remind us of the importance of these in our
daily lives, and that we are morally bound to live by them. However, charity in
this instance is often referred to as love, which is to remind us that although
we are obligated to practice faith, hope, and charity, we are to do so not out of
obligation but in a character of love.
What about all the hieroglyphical emblems of the third degree that are not
explained in the short-form lecture? Have you taught them in your lodges? If
they are not being taught, how can we possibly be living up to the meanings
behind them, which are part of our obligations?
It is no secret to the world that we Masons care for one another; that we
help each other and go out of our way to not injure each other. But again, there’s
more to it than that. I contend that we are morally bound or obligated to not only
support each other during times of distress, and to avoid injuring one another,
but the reverse is true and we should go out of our way to lift each other up. I
stand before you an example of what I mean. Most Worshipful Brill and I have
known each other for well over a decade, and he knows the struggles I have
with Parkinson’s and how it has limited my ability to do some of the things
that I enjoyed doing prior to my diagnosis. To some, he would be fulfilling his
obligation by simply not talking bad about me or not putting me down due to
my disability. But he went a step further in fulfilling his obligation. He didn’t
see me as a brother who had limitations. Instead he saw me as one who still has
the ability to contribute to the craft. How well is, of course, a matter of opinion.
Nevertheless, in so doing, he gave me purpose and validated that I still have a
role in the fraternity. It’s a gesture for which I am eternally grateful. Perhaps in
your lodges there is a brother who, though he wants to participate, is reluctant
to do so because he has trouble with memorization or is a bit hesitant to take
on a formal leadership role. Perhaps he has physical disabilities that limit what
he is able to do. Find a place for him. It is your moral obligation as a leader of
the fraternity to do so. Perhaps he can be your chaplain or a steward. Maybe he
can head a committee for you. While it is your stated obligation to not harm
him, it is also your moral obligation as a brother to lift him up and show him
he is valued.
The world knows we stand for brotherly love, relief, and truth. To us, truth
includes reaching out to a brother when he is falling short and not meeting

standards; to provide guidance and counseling when a brother has erred. This
is not easy to do. Most people, us included, are uncomfortable pointing out to
someone the error of their way. Even fewer of us are comfortable hearing that we
have gone astray. So here we have an example where our stated obligation—to
point out errors—includes an unstated moral duty to receive that information.
How can we make it more comfortable for us to be open to criticism? I can tell
you what works for me. Find that one brother with whom you really connect and
make him what I call your traveling brother. I have one and he’s in the audience
today, and rest assured he will let me know how I did on delivering this oration.
Develop such a relationship with your traveling brother that he’s comfortable
calling out your errors and you are comfortable hearing it from him, and vice
versa. Use that brother as a sounding board if someone else points out an area
in which you have fallen short, to validate or mitigate the issue. The more open
we come to receiving guidance and correction, the more open other brothers
will be to give it. Such openness is critical if we are to meet our goal of taking
good men and making them better.
Another area that is oftentimes forgotten is the moral duties and obligations we assume at installation. Masters of the different lodges, do you recall
that during your installation you agreed that you would diligently search, and
from time to time cause to be read in your lodge the constitution of the Grand
Lodge of California? I won’t ask for a show of hands, but how many of you have
actually had portions of the constitution read in your lodge? If you have not,
then you have missed out on a portion of fulfilling your obligation. What about
all those edicts and communications that you receive from the grand lodge and
the grand master, after they are read in your lodge do you act on them? It is part
of your obligations to do so.
Brothers, I mention these things only to demonstrate that fulfilling our
obligations, both stated and moral, is a deep and involved process. I hope it
is evident to you by now that we could spend perhaps the remainder of the
weekend simply discussing the ways that we need to work and live to fulfill all
our obligations. But we will not do that.
Instead, I will leave you with a thought. How can you measure how well you
are doing in fulfilling your obligations? Well here is a challenge for you. When
you go home at the end of this Annual Communication, spend some time going
over the charges, the perambulations, and the formal obligations contained
within the California cipher. Consider the working tools and emblems. Read the
constitution and the by-laws of your lodge. Contemplate what you are formally
and morally obligated to do for some four million brothers around the world,
the vast majority of whom you have never met. Ask yourself what kind of man
would I want that person to be that I would cheerfully fulfill all my obligations
for him without ever meeting or getting to know him. Then go to your mirror,
look at the face staring back at you and honestly ask yourself the question, Am
I that kind of man?
Brethren, thank you for your attention and I hope I have challenged you

154

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

and given you some food for thought. Most Worshipful Brill, thank you so much
for the confidence you have displayed in me throughout this past Masonic year.
May God bless America, the Grand Lodge of Freemasons of California, and each
and every one of you. Thank you.
Respectfully submitted,
David G. Rathgeber, Grand Orator

2023 GRAND LODGE LEGISLATION

GRAND MASTER’S DECISIONS AND
RECOMMENDATIONS
Grand Master Brill’s Recommendation No. 1:
Sets Lodge Anniversary Date as the Earlier of the
Lodge’s Dispensation Date or Charter Date
The California Masonic Code (“Code”) states that the anniversary of the
formation of a Lodge is the date of the Grand Master’s dispensation to the Lodge.
A Grand Master’s dispensation is the Lodge’s authority to open, meet and work.
Using dispensation as the marker for a Lodge’s anniversary is problematic. A
number of existing Lodges do not have dispensation dates because their formations did not require it. In the future, certain new Lodges may not be required to
receive dispensation from the Grand Master. For example, under the Code, our
Grand Lodge may issue a Charter to a Lodge without prior dispensation if that
Lodge was chartered by another Grand Lodge recognized by our Grand Lodge.
The Code’s confusion with respect to a Lodge’s anniversary was evident in
the 1990’s when many of the Fraternity’s original Lodges were planning their
150th anniversary celebrations. The Grand Lodge Executive Committees of that
era recognized a Lodge’s anniversary as the earlier of the Lodge’s dispensation
date or its “Charter date,” the date the Lodge was issued its Charter.
Now, approximately twenty-five years later, Lodges are preparing for their
175th anniversaries and the issue is again upon us. Thus, the time is ripe to
adjust the Code. I recommend that the Code be revised to state that a Lodge’s
anniversary is the earliest of the date of:
(i) the dispensation by the Grand Master to the Lodge, (ii) the Charter
issued to the Lodge by our Grand Lodge, or (iii) the dispensation or charter
issued to the Lodge by a Grand Lodge of another jurisdiction recognized by
our Grand Lodge.
If you adopt this recommendation, Section 801.010 of the Code will be
amended as marked:

158

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

159

§801.010. FORMATION.
A Lodge can be formed only by authority of a dispensation from the Grand
Master, or of a Charter issued by Grand Lodge. A Charter shall not be
granted to any Lodge until it has worked a time under dispensation, and has
exhibited to Grand Lodge satisfactory evidence of its Masonic capability.
Grand Lodge has the sole right to grant or direct a Charter to be issued to
worth Master Masons if qualified. If any Lodge duly chartered by any Grand
Body recognized by this Jurisdiction shall, with the consent and approval
of such Grand Body, petition Grand Lodge for a Charter, Grand Lodge shall
have the power to issue a Charter to the Lodge upon such terms and in
such manner as it deems proper without Dispensation having been issued.
The anniversary of the formation of the Lodge is the earliest of the
date of the issuance of the Dispensation by the Grand Master, not the
date of the Charter issued to the Lodge by Grand Lodge, or the date of the
dispensation or charter issued to the Lodge by a Grand Body recognized
by this Jurisdiction.
Amendment to the Ordinances.
5/6 affirmative vote required for adoption.

Resolution No. 22-02:
Gives the Grand Master the Right to Grant the Title

The proponents of this Resolution seek to give the Grand Master the
right to grant the title of Past Master upon a member that does not complete
his term as Master due to the suspension or revocation of his Lodge’s charter.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, Lodge Charter Suspensions do happen from time to time; and,
WHEREAS, A Master of a Lodge may not be able to finish his elected term due
to a Charter Suspension; and,
WHEREAS, The Charter suspension circumstances may have nothing to do
with the Master; and,
WHEREAS, A Master has served and performed his duties to serve the Lodge
in spite of the Lodge’s Issues,
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 404.120 of the California
Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§404.120. POWERS OF THE GRAND MASTER.
The Grand Master may:
A. During the interval between Annual Communications of Grand Lodge,
exercise all executive powers of the Grand Lodge, except the power
to grant charters;
B. Convene any Lodge, preside therein, inspect its proceedings, and
compel its conformity to Masonic usage;

appertaining to the duties of his office;

E. Issue edicts requiring conformity with the requirements of this Code,
the General Regulations of Masonry and the Ritual;
F.

Make Masons at sight or at will only in a regular Lodge with the unanimous consent of the members present; and

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Section 805.020 of the California Masonic
Code be amended as marked:
§805.020. PAST MASTERS.
The title of Past Master applies only to a member who:
A. Has been regularly elected or named in a Charter as Master of a chartered Lodge in this Jurisdiction (other than a Research Lodge or a
Historic Lodge);
B. Has been installed as Master of a chartered Lodge in this Jurisdiction
(other than a Research Lodge or a Historic Lodge);
C. Has served until the installation of his successor, except in the case of
death or, consolidation, the suspension or revocation of such Lodge’s
charter, as provided below, or has served until his own installation as
Master of such Lodge for the subsequent year; and
D. Is at the time in good standing in a Constituent Lodge.
If a Master resigns before the installation of his successor, he forfeits
all right to the title of Past Master and to membership in Grand Lodge,
unless otherwise qualified.
If a member has been regularly elected or named in a Charter and
installed as Master of a chartered Lodge in this Jurisdiction and dies while
serving as Master, he may by resolution of his Lodge be designated as a
Past Master.
A member in good standing in a Constituent Lodge who has been regularly elected or named in a Charter and installed as Master of a chartered
Lodge in this Jurisdiction shall have the title of Past Master, if the Lodge
consolidated while he was serving as Master and he did not become Master

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

161

of the consolidated Lodge.
A member in good standing in a Constituent Lodge who has been regularly elected or named in a Charter and installed as Master of a chartered
Lodge in this Jurisdiction may have the title of Past Master if the Lodge’s
charter was suspended or revoked while he was serving as Master only if
deemed appropriate and so granted by the Grand Master.
A member in good standing in a Constituent Lodge who has been
regularly elected or named in a Charter, installed as Master and served
until the installation of his successor in a chartered Lodge in another
Jurisdiction may take the honorary title of “Past Master,” but he shall not
thereby become a member of this Grand Lodge.
If Grand Lodge charters a Lodge formed by a Grand Body recognized
by this Grand Lodge, it may by resolution provide that the title of Past
Master shall apply to the Past Masters of such Lodge and entitle them to
the rights and privileges of Past Masters of this Jurisdiction.

Resolution No. 22-04:
Modifies the Threshold Amount of a Contract
Requiring the Approval of the Grand Lodge Committee
on Masonic Properties
The proponents of this Resolution seek to increase the threshold amount
of a contract requiring the approval of the Grand Lodge Committee on Masonic
Properties from $25,000 to $50,000.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, California Masonic Code Section 406.060.D requires prior consent

162

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

of the Grand Lodge Committee on Masonic Properties if the expected cost of
any construction, alteration, improvement, replacement, repair, or maintenance
to a Masonic building is in excess of $25,000;
WHEREAS, this amount has not been increased since the year 2000;
WHEREAS, the California Construction Cost Index maintained by the
California Department of General Services has increased by more than 127%
over the last 22 years;
WHEREAS, with the rise in construction costs, the present threshold of $25,000
is not appropriate for current conditions, being no longer adequate to cover
many of the routine projects that Masonic Hall Associations are required to
undertake;
WHEREAS, raising the threshold would reduce the burden of work unnecessarily incurred by Masonic Hall Associations, by the Grand Lodge Committee
on Masonic Properties and by the Grand Lodge Office staff, together with the
expenses associated therewith;
WHEREAS, removing barriers to the improvement, repair and maintenance
of Masonic properties would assist in improving positive awareness of the
fraternity and further the aims of the 2025 Strategic Plan;
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that Section 406.060 of the California
Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§406.060. MASONIC PROPERTIES.
The Committee on Masonic Properties shall consist of not less than five
nor more than twenty members. It shall examine and approve all details
regarding any contract involving a Lodge, Masonic Hall Association, committee, partnership or corporation or other entity representing itself to be
Masonic in character, or operating for the benefit of a Constituent Lodge
or Constituent Lodges for:
A. Any option or contract for the purchase of real property;
B. The encumbrance of real property;
C. The lease of real property, as lessor or lessee, for more than three years;
D. A contract for or commencement of the construction, alteration,
improvement, replacement, repair, or maintenance of real property if
the expected cost is in excess of $25,000 $50,000; and
E. Any option or contract regarding the sale or listing for sale of real
property.
The committee shall, subject to the approval of the Grand Master,

establish rules and regulations governing the processing of applications
for committee approval.
The committee shall review the reports of transactions of Masonic
Hall Associations submitted to the Grand Secretary as provided in Section
900.050 of this Code and may give counsel and advise concerning the
operation of those Masonic Hall Associations.
The committee shall also advise Lodges and the Grand Lodge on matters of taxation with respect to income, property, sales and employment
taxes.

Resolution No. 23-02:
Permits a Member to Be the Secretary
of More Than one Lodge
The proponents of this Resolution seek to permit a member to hold the office
of Secretary in more than one Lodge.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, the Secretary of a Lodge is limited to holding that office in a single
Lodge; and
WHEREAS, a new Secretary often takes years to learn the job; and
WHEREAS, experienced Secretaries are hard to find; and
WHEREAS, a smaller Lodge whose Secretary vacates the position will frequently
have difficulty finding a replacement; and
WHEREAS, any Lodge in a remote area whose Secretary vacates the position
will frequently have difficulty finding a replacement; and

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

169

WHEREAS, much of the Secretary’s work can now be done on-line through
the Grand Lodge website;
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 805.010 of the California
Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§805.010. OFFICERS.
The officers of a Lodge are Master, Senior Warden, Junior Warden,
Treasurer, Secretary, Chaplain, Senior Deacon, Junior Deacon, Marshal,
Senior Steward, Junior Steward, Tiler and other officers as the Lodge may
deem proper to appoint. The Master, Senior Warden and Junior Warden,
Treasurer and Secretary shall be elected in conformity with this Code. The
other officers shall be appointed by the Master. Any Master Mason in good
standing, whether or not a member of the Lodge, may be appointed Tiler or
Organist. All other officers shall be members in good standing of the Lodge.
A member may not be Master, or Warden or Secretary, or any combination thereof, of two or more Lodges (other than Research Lodges and
Historic Lodges) at the same time. No one may hold more than one office
in a Lodge at the same time.
The title of Master applies not only to him who has been elected and
installed as Master, but to either of the Wardens while acting as Master.

Resolution No. 23-03:

B. Examining a candidate in the Candidate’s Lecture of any degree;

Allows Special Meetings to Be Held on the
Same Day as a Stated Meeting

C. Conferring of degrees;
D. Funeral service;

The proponents of this Resolution seek to allow Special Meetings to be held
on the same day as a Stated Meeting.

E. Installation;

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

G. After dispensation from the Grand Master:

WHEREAS, Section 807.010 of the California Masonic Code states that “No
Special Meeting shall be held on the same day as a Stated Meeting”; and
WHEREAS, certain business such as the conferring of the Fellow Craft or
Master Mason degrees, conducting a funeral service in a Lodge of Master
Masons, installing officers in a Lodge of Master Masons, and the consideration
of relief of a worthy Mason in a Lodge of Master Masons cannot be done during
a Stated Meeting, and
WHEREAS, Masons often travel long distances to attend Lodge meetings,
occasionally making it desirable (especially for seniors and plural members)
to consolidate business to Stated Meeting dates in order to reduce the cost,
burden, and additional travel risks of returning for extra meetings, and
WHEREAS, this resolution, if adopted, will permit but not require Lodges to
confer any degree and conduct other Fellow Craft and Master Mason business
on the same date as a Stated Meeting, and
WHEREAS, this resolution, if adopted, will not compel any Constituent Lodge
to change their current practice of holding Special Meetings on days other than
Stated Meeting days,
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 807.010 of the California
Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§807.010. SPECIAL MEETINGS.
Except as provided in Section 807.020 of this Code, a Lodge may hold such
Special Meetings in addition to its Stated Meeting on such dates and at such
times as it determines or the Master shall direct. A Special Meeting may
be held on the same day but not at the same time as a Stated Meeting or
other Special Meeting. A postponed Stated Meeting shall not be considered
to be a Special Meeting.
Only the following business may be conducted at a Special Meeting:
A. Collections or appropriations for charity;

171

F.

Electing a representative to the Annual or a Special Communication
of the Grand Lodge; or
1.

Balloting for and conferring the degrees upon an applicant without
reference to a committee, or

2.

Receiving and acting upon the application of a rejected applicant
within less than 12 months after the date of his rejection.

If the Grand Master determines that assembling the required number of
persons for holding a Special Meeting is prohibited by competent local, state
or national authority, the Grand Master may authorize the Lodge to hold a
Special Meeting through the use of conference telephone, electronic video
screen communication or electronic transmission so long as each member
of the Lodge participating in the meeting can communicate with all of the
other members concurrently and each member participating is provided the
means of participating in all matters before the meeting, including, without
limitation, the capacity to propose, or to interpose an objection to, a specific action to be taken by the Lodge. Such meetings shall be held without
the Lodge opening and closing ceremonies in the Ritual and without any
other esoteric or secret portion of the Ritual. The following business may
not be conducted at any such meeting: balloting, examining a candidate in
the Candidate’s Lecture of any degree or conferring of degrees. The Grand
Master may make provision for voting if a written ballot is requested on
any matter, for notice to the Lodge members of the date, time and means
of electronic access to the meeting, for tiling such a meeting and for any

in this Code. Constituent Lodges whose long- established ritualistic work

Resolution No. 23-06:
Changes the Years of Service from the Date
Raised to the Date Initiated
The proponents of this Resolution seek to change a member’s years of service
to be measured from the date of his initiation rather than the date of his raising.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, the proponents of this resolution seek to credit masonic members
with their service time spent prior to being raised a Master Mason. It is the
opinion of the proponents that if we are going to require Entered Apprentices
and Fellow Craft Masons to pay the same dues as Master Masons they are
entitled to time spent before being raised;
WHEREAS, we also should consider with our stated business meetings being
conducted in the First Degree there is not or at least should not be a big rush
to make a candidate a Master Mason before he has had the time to become
educated in the degree he owns. Our job as Lodge officers should not be just to
make Master Masons in the shortest time possible, but to mentor and educate
our Entered Apprentices and Fellow Crafts to become Master Masons on their
own time when they and their mentors believe they are ready.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 804.630 of the California
Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§804.630. LODGE MEMBERSHIP OF APPLICANTS FOR THE DEGREES.
Membership in the Lodge to which a candidate has been elected to the
degree of Master Mason shall commence as of the date of his raising and
his years of service shall be deemed to have commenced as of the date of
his initiation.
Respectfully submitted,
s/ Gary K. Jackson, PM, No. 857
s/ Charles T. Malear Jr., PM, No. 827
s/ Jay D. Clark, PM, No. 857
s/ Michael B. Thoms, PM, No. 426
Amendment to the Ordinances.
5/6 affirmative vote required for adoption.
Gary K. Jackson is authorized to represent and act for the Resolution.
