REPORT OF THE
BOARD OF TRUSTEES
Masonic Homes of California
For an institution as longstanding and venerable as the Masonic
Homes of California, the COVID-19 pandemic was yet another challenge to
surmount—one of many its endured over the many decades. Now, on its 125th
anniversary, the Masonic Homes is emerging with brand new facilities and
forward-looking programming that will enable the organization to tackle the
challenges of a post-pandemic world and address the changing needs of its
membership and their families.
While life is largely back to normal for the 285 residents on the Masonic
Homes’ campuses in Union City and Covina, those communities have undergone some big changes lately. Since the Pavilion opened in 2021 in Union City
to bring memory care and assisted-living support to residents of the Masonic
Homes, Acacia Creek, and the wider public, the Wollenberg and Adams building,
originally built in the early 1960s, have both undergone a complete renovation.
That includes the addition of new memory care and assisted-living residences
in Wollenberg and a reconfigured common area in Adams that provides additional social space for our residents, including a game room, refreshment area,
theater/card room, and dining area. This work, along with new landscaping and
the addition of the veteran’s memorial fountain honoring residents who served
in the armed forces, was completed in 2023.
Meanwhile, in Covina, the long-awaited health center has been completed
and licensing is underway to house 32 residents with memory care and longand short-term skilled nursing needs, rounding out the services provided on
that campus. Systemwide, these projects have increased capacity by 58 percent
while greatly expanding the share of beds licensed for memory care and skilled
nursing, two rapidly growing needs. (This year, the Lorber skilled nursing facility in Union City, which served 121 residents, was recognized by U.S. News and
World Report as a Best Nursing Home. It also maintained its coveted five-star
rating from Medicare Compare.) For the first time in decades, the doors of the
Masonic Homes are open with zero waitlist.
Expanding services has emerged as a major theme for the Masonic Homes,
and not just on campus. Our community-based services, the Masonic Center
for Youth and Families and Masonic Outreach Services, have grown rapidly to

180

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

serve clients throughout the state both in-person and remotely. In 2023, MYCAF
worked with 1,553 clients—more than three times its caseload in 2019—while
MOS fielded 2,945 calls to the Masonic Assistance hotline this year from Masons
needing advice, resources, and emergency funds through the Distressed Worthy
Brother Relief Fund. It ultimately supported 378 clients with case management
or financial assistance. Lodge Outreach Services also resumed, with meetings
held throughout the state that trained 189 members of the fraternity in 2023 to
provide support to members locally. In a single online event, Masonic Assistance
staff presented to more than 400 Masons, widows, and family members about
the services they have access to through the Masonic Homes, including the
Masonic Value Network, which provides members with prescription discounts,
referral benefits for home care, and more.
The Masonic Center for Youth and Families has seen an exponential
increase in demand for its mental health services. Since the beginning of the
pandemic, community mental health providers like MCYAF have seen a surge
in demand for services. To meet that need, MCYAF has increased its support
to Masons across the lifespan, developing partnerships with the Masonic youth
orders, making presentations to spouses and partners at leadership retreats,
and providing direct services to staff and seniors living at the Masonic Homes.
It has also partnered with several outside organizations, including the Pomona
Unified School District and the California Scottish Rite, to bring educational
assessments, therapy, and other mental health services to those communities.
It also became a mental health partner with Kaiser Permanente this year.
Partnerships like those are a key to the future of the Masonic Homes.
For example, in order to meet the growing demand for skilled caregivers, the
organization joined in 2023 with Unitek College, a provider of high-quality
nursing and technical education for the senior care industry, to develop the
“Masonic Homes Academy.” Through this partnership, the Masonic Homes
will provide scholarships and training opportunities through Unitek to existing
and prospective staff members who looking to advance their careers and obtain
higher-level professional certification. The academy recently graduated its first
class of eight new nursing assistants, all of whom have accepted jobs with the
Masonic Homes. The Masonic Homes also continues to collaborate with the
Alzheimer’s Association, the Children’s Advocacy Center of Covina, and other
local civic and healthcare organizations. Within the fraternity, the organization
is committed to working closely with the Masonic Communities and Services
Association and the RiteCare Language Centers of the Scottish Rite.
Looking forward, the board and staff initiated a few notable multi-year
projects in 2023, including a further expansion of our services to reach more
people, an expanded vision for our delivery of mental health services, a re-branding initiative to better align the Masonic Homes’ name and logos with the vast
array of services it offers, and a deep exploration of the organization’s pricing,
procedures, and services. In each case, the goal is to become the first call our
members make when they are in need.

Meanwhile, President and CEO Gary Charland announced his retirement
in July 2023 after more than 10 years with the Masonic Homes. As a result, the
board spent much of the past year engaged in an exhaustive nationwide search
for his replacement. This summer, the board was pleased to announce that Terry
Quigley was appointed to helm the organization. Quigley was previously senior
vice president and COO of Episcopal Communities and Services in San Diego,
where she oversaw a network that included three continuing-care retirement
residences, one assisted living facility, and one affordable housing community
that together served some 700 residents. Her successful tenure there, and her
extensive career in senior living, made her the right choice to lead the Masonic
Homes into its next phase. We look forward to her vision and leadership as we
move forward.
The board wishes to thank Gary Charland for the decade of exemplary
vision, service, and leadership he’s given to the Masonic Homes. His campus
master plan was wide-reaching and ambitious, and we now enjoy the fruits of
the years of planning and execution that went into it. Under his direction, the
Masonic Homes of California has grown its range of services through MOS and
seen MCYAF expand to Covina and statewide, reaching more Masons, children,
and families than ever before. He helped build cutting-edge memory care supports, introduced the Masonic Value Network, and built strong partnerships
across the industry and local community. He led our organization through the
most challenging period in the history of the senior health industry with an
unwavering focus on resident and staff safety. His vision has forever changed
the Masonic Homes and set the direction for the future of the organization.
As I complete my final year as chairman of the board, I’m proud and humbled by the good work this board has done for our residents, our fraternity,
and our community. At the same time, I look forward to a bright future at the
Masonic Homes of California. Thank you for the opportunity to serve an organization that means so much to me.
Respectfully submitted,
Board of Trustees
Larry L. Adamson, PGM, Chairman
Ara Maloyan, Vice Chairman
Terry Quigley, President & Chief Executive Officer
Joseph P. Pritchard, Vice President
Charles P. Cross, Treasurer
Allan L. Casalou, Secretary

Acacia Creek Retirement Community
The economic fallout from the pandemic continues to reverberate at
senior living communities across the country. Unfortunately, Acacia Creek has
not been immune to these trends. And while vacancy rates both here and nationally are beginning to creep back up, they remain well below pre-pandemic levels.
Over the past year, the board of Acacia Creek Retirement Community,
which is now in its 13th year of operation, has focused its attention squarely
on increasing its census count. Those efforts are paying off. Since resuming
in-person prospect visits in mid-2022, tour activity has increased month over
month. The board, together with the Masonic Homes of California, has also
engaged an outside consultant to train and augment its sales team and help
develop new prospecting events and marketing materials. Together, we have
implemented new benchmarks, timelines, and marketing strategies based on
industry standards. Thanks to that work, we’re seeing positive results and
improving the volume of quality sales leads, which is essential for establishing strong occupancy projections. In the meantime, the Masonic Homes of
California has generously offered more Acacia Creek apartments to its residents
on an assignment of asset basis to welcome more Masons into independent
living on our shared campus.
Meanwhile, the board and staff of Acacia Creek have remained steadfast
in their commitment to providing residents with an active and meaningful
life. That promise is supported by a strategic plan adopted in 2022 centered
around four themes: quality of life, operational integrity, board engagement,
and Masonic connections.
The ﬁrst theme, quality of life, represents the well-being, safety, and happiness of residents—which has always been and will always be the most important
goal at Acacia Creek. In 2023, that was reflected in the TK percent rate at which
residents reported their overall satisfaction with life on campus. The second
theme is operational integrity, or the management of ﬁscal responsibilities.
The third theme is board engagement, aimed at developing a culture in which
members of the board participate actively in the Acacia Creek community. The
ﬁnal theme, Masonic connections, aligns Acacia Creek’s strategic plan with
that of the fraternity.

208

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

Acacia Creek remains a special place to age and grow. It is one of just 15
senior communities nationwide to be certified as a Center for Successful Aging.
Its residents demonstrate through annual reviews that they enjoy better health,
nutrition, and rates of physical activity than do seniors at comparable communities, or even in their own homes.
Acacia Creek’s partnership with Masterpiece LLC, a national organization
providing thought leadership and programming on physical and mental wellness for seniors, remains a key part of that success. Through Masterpiece LLC
programs, Acacia Creek residents and staﬀ are empowered to pursue new skills,
physical activities, opportunities for personal fulfillment, and opportunities to
contribute to the wider community. Since 2019, the Acacia Creek leadership
team has focused on training all team members and their families on Successful
Aging goals to encourage healthy living and promote job satisfaction.
That is particularly important against the backdrop of industry-wide staffing shortages. The team management concept in place at Acacia Creek, which
includes providing opportunities for continuing education through a sponsored
scholarship program, is working. In the 2023 team member satisfaction survey,
Acacia Creek team members rated their work experience at a 95 percent satisfaction level.
Numbers like those demonstrate why Acacia Creek is such a rewarding
place to work and live. Its mission, to provide seniors with a vibrant community
in which they can grow and thrive, is unchanged. Despite the major challenges
posed by the pandemic and the protracted recovery of the entire senior living
industry, the board is committed to fulfilling that vision.
The board wishes to extend its sincere and continued appreciation to Chuck
Major, president of Acacia Creek, who has maintained a high level of morale
and accountability of the team. Together, they helped maintain the high-quality
lifestyle for the residents that is the goal of Acacia Creek.
I would like to thank the members of the Acacia Creek board, the members
of the Grand Lodge Executive Committee, and the Grand Lodge staff. We especially want to thank the Masonic Homes board for their continued investment
in our success in these challenges financial times. We look forward to a new
era of partnership with Masonic Homes. We are excited about our future, and
together we look forward to ensuring the continued success in support of the
community and mission of Acacia Creek.
Respectfully submitted,
Board of Directors
Jeffrey M. Schimsky, Chairman
Charles W. Major, President
Charles P. Cross, Treasurer
Allan L. Casalou, Secretary

REPORT OF THE

California Masonic Foundation
The past year has been one of great change for the California Masonic
Foundation. Having completed its landmark, five-year Let’s Write the Future campaign in 2022, during which the membership rallied to donate more than $7 million
for youth literacy programs and seniors at the Masonic Homes, the Foundation
began transitioning toward an exciting new “place-based” philanthropic strategy.
As both the fundraising arm of the fraternity and the primary vehicle
through which California Masons put their values into action, the Foundation
is committed to making the greatest positive impact possible in our communities. This year, for the first time, the Foundation began pursuing a new approach
to doing just that. And as always, the Masons of California have responded by
supporting us at every step of the way.
Rather than spread our time, energy, and charitable dollars around the
entire state, the Foundation worked to bring as many of its resources and
relationships as possible to bear on a single community. This year, that place
was San Diego. As part of this work, the Foundation leveraged its connections
with existing local partners and developed new ones—while at the same time
convening like-minded organizations to expand their reach.
This is a new approach to community service for the Foundation and one
that leans into the kind of relationship-building that Masons do best. Not only
was the Foundation able to build on its existing programs in that community,
like Raising a Reader and Masons4Mitts, but also develop new ones alongside
new and old partners. The result is tangible—and incredibly impactful.
Our work in San Diego this year included several components. The first
came in January, when, alongside our longtime college readiness partners Reality
Changers of San Diego and the San Diego Padres Foundation, the Foundation
announced the launch of the Johnny Ritchey Scholarship Program. This scholarship provides 10 awards of up to $10,000 to students who have encountered and
overcome significant personal adversity in their pursuit of higher education. The
program honors Ritchey, the “Jackie Robinson of the West Coast,” who in 1948
became the first Black player in the Pacific Coast League. In addition to providing
a wonderful opportunity for promising students and honoring an important
figure in San Diego history, this program demonstrates what’s possible when

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

211

the Foundation brings partners like the Padres and Reality Changers together.
That approach also led the Foundation to perhaps its biggest success story
of the past year: A three-year gift totaling $390,000 to the San Diego Unified
School District to support its college, career, and technical education department. Through this new program, students from under-resourced communities
in San Diego will be able to learn about and pursue well-paid careers in the
trades, with a particular focus on automotive repair and building construction.
This program, inspired by the Working Tools Scholarship, shows students that
a four-year college degree is not always the best or only path to a good job. It
was thanks to the Foundation’s longstanding relationship with Raising a Reader
and SDUSD—the second-biggest district in the state, and one in which nearly
60 percent of students qualify for reduced-price lunch—as well as nearby
community colleges, community organizations like Reality Changers, and the
local relationships we have through members of our Public Education Advisory
Committees that the Foundation was able to deliver on this major pledge.
Both of those programs are aimed at setting young people up for success in
the future. But the Foundation understands that supporting public education
isn’t just about supporting kids. It also requires that teachers and administrators
have the resources they need to be their best. With that in mind, the Foundation
and its partners at the San Diego Padres Community Foundation this year began
work on an ambitious project to reinvigorate single school: Perkins Elementary.
The problems at Perkins, a K-8 school in the Barrio Logan neighborhood, are a
microcosm of the biggest challenges facing California schools today. Thirty-seven
percent of kids at Perkins are currently experiencing homelessness. Two-thirds
are considered chronically absent. Most do not meet grade-level standards in
English or math. Virtually every family at Perkins is living in poverty. The result
is that students there are living through unbelievable trauma and stress every day.
It also means that teachers and administrators are dealing not just with students’
grades and test scores, but also more basic issues like hunger, safety, and health.
Together, the California Masonic Foundation and San Diego Padres
Community Foundation have adopted Perkins Elementary. Working with school
officials, we have identified several infrastructure projects at the school in
desperate need of renovation in order to make students and staff feel safe and
secure, and to create a welcoming environment in which they can learn and grow.
These efforts serve as concrete examples of our Masonic values. We are
proud of this project and what it represents and believe the strategy behind
it is one we can build on, replicate, and expand to other communities in need
throughout our state. In subsequent years, we plan to use the same philosophy to
bring our network of local partners and expertise to other communities in need.
Of course, this work is only part of the broader portfolio of efforts the
California Masonic Foundation undertakes each year. Elsewhere, the Foundation
continued its successful charitable programs, which are summarized below.
Investment in Success Scholarships: Our longest-standing scholarship
program continued in 2023 with the awarding of $270,000 in gifts to 174 students

212

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

to pursue higher education. These gifts are given to young people who have faced
unique challenges in their lives and have displayed the grit, determination, and
passion to continue to pursue their dreams of higher education. The Investment
in Success award is typically the only scholarship they will ever receive.
C.E. Towne Masonic Award: This scholarship, launched in 2019 in collaboration with the Prince Hall Grand Lodge of California, has grown into one
of the Foundation’s largest awards. In 2023, it distributed a total of $228,000
to 24 students. Since its inception, the C.E. Towne Masonic Award has been
given to 102 students for a total of $710,000.
Masonic Youth Leadership Scholarship: This year, the Foundation closed
in on $1 million in all-time support for this scholarship benefitting outstanding
members of the Masonic youth orders, including $112,000 in 2023. Founded
by the Most Worshipful M. David Perry in 2016, this scholarship recognizes
members of the Masonic youth orders who make great sacrifices during their
time as leaders in our jurisdiction. Altogether, the Foundation issued $860,000
in scholarships to 221 students.
Raising a Reader: The Foundation is nearing its goal of bringing the
national youth literacy nonprofit’s family reading program to 1,000 classrooms
in California. By the end of the 2023–24 school year, we will have introduced
Raising a Reader to 941 classrooms in the lowest-performing quartile of the state
and expect to hit the 1,000 mark by spring of 2024—an important milestone
and one that demonstrates the enormous impact this program has on some of
the state’s most under-resourced communities. Thanks to all the members who
have contributed this this important effort over the years.
Masons4Mitts: Coming off a record-setting season in 2022, California
Masons’ all-time gifts to Masons4Mitts surpassed $2 million this season, driven
by record giving in three of our four MLB regions. Spurred by new and energetic
leadership among our team captains, Masons set fundraising marks in Northern
California ($126,824), L.A ($72,069), and Orange County ($47,042). Overall
fundraising also set a new single-season high, at $286,580. Since launching
Masons4Mitts in 2008, the Foundation has donated more than 100,000 mitts
to young people, removing a major stigma for those who might otherwise be
unable to participate, and bringing enriching summer programs to communities
around the state.
Fellow Craft Degree Pin: Beginning in 2021, the Foundation launched a
new initiative to better familiarize members with the programs of the California
Masonic Foundation by connecting them to the lessons of the Fellow Craft degree.
As part of that, the Foundation developed a special pin to be presented to candidates at the conclusion of their second-degree conferral. During that ceremony,
a representative of the Foundation delivers a speech outlining its longstanding
commitment to education and learning. In 2023, members of the Public Education
Advisory Committees delivered these pins to 85 new Fellow Craft Masons. This is
an encouraging start, but we hope to do more in the coming year to expand this
effort and ensure the Fellow Craft pin is a regular part of every Fellow Craft degree.

Annual Fund Giving: With the completion of the Let’s Write the Future
campaign in 2022 and leadership-level gifts largely fulfilled, overall giving to the
Foundation’s annual fund was expectedly down in 2023, totaling $1,070,676 as
of August 17. The average member gift was also down slightly from last year’s
record high, at about $285. However, the number of members who made a gift
to the Foundation was up, as was the percentage of members giving and the
total number of lodge officer gifts. Recurring online gifts and Grand Master’s
Circle-level gifts were also up slightly.
On balance, 2023 has been a successful year and one in which the Foundation
was able to demonstrate the efficacy of its place-based giving strategy, support
several deserving organizations and individuals, and address our important
positive awareness goals. Our success is measured by our ability to impact
lives. The support of the membership is what allows us to do that—and in so
doing, demonstrate to our communities that Freemasonry is a force for good.
The board would like to thank the staff of the California Masonic Foundation,
led by its president, Doug Ismail. The Foundation’s staff, including Denise Avila,
Joshua Castro, Greg Cherry, Candler Gibson, and Rich Kellogg, have a combined
experience with our fraternity exceeding 80 years. Their work on behalf of the
Foundation has been critical to its success—and we would like to express our
gratitude for their hard work.
Respectfully submitted,
Board of Trustees

California Masonic Memorial Temple
On just about every front, the past year has been a successful one for the
California Masonic Memorial Temple. Financial performance has been strong.
Activity at the Nob Hill Masonic Center has returned to pre-pandemic levels.
The 2030 capital plan is progressing on track. And most importantly, the board
of trustees is looking forward by developing plans for even more types of programming to increase revenue and awareness of the home of California Masonry.
The CMMT plays an important role for the fraternity. In addition to serving
as the headquarters of the Grand Lodge of California and host of the Annual
Communication, net revenue generated through events and rentals of the
building supports the efforts of the California Masonic Foundation. With Live
Nation returning to a full calendar of events—including 42 concerts, 29 comedy
shows, six speaker events, and 12 private events—and other financial projects
proceeding according to plan, the CMMT was able to make a distribution of
$322,737 to the Foundation.
That number is poised to grow. This year, the board of the CMMT and
Live Nation amended their conditional use permit to allow for 12 additional
non-music events per year, a move that was approved by the San Francisco
Planning Commission on June 27. As part of that agreement, Live Nation agreed
to several new operating upgrades that will mitigate neighborhood impacts.
Further, the CMMT is looking into opportunities to generate more public
rentals of Freemasons’ Hall in the coming year, focusing on small, high-end
private events and weddings. Currently, 10 Masonic organizations meet at
Freemasons’ Hall, including six lodges under the Grand Lodge of California,
three lodges operating under other grand lodges, and a chapter of the Royal Arch.
Over the past year, the board has focused on ways to use the CMMT to
increase public awareness of Freemasonry. As part of the 2025 Fraternity Plan,
the board identified four key elements in that effort: messaging and content
planning, improving its online presence, building activation efforts, and implementing on-site programming. Thanks to the efforts of the Grand Lodge communications department, the first three parts of that plan have been achieved.
Visitors to the CMMT now encounter QR codes posted within and outside
the building, which direct them toward information about the history of the

REPORT OF THE BOARD OF TRUSTEES
Nob Hill Masonic Center
Nestled atop the iconic Nob Hill in San Francisco stands the California
Masonic Memorial Temple, an architectural marvel that has been a part of
the city’s landscape for 65 years and serves as the general headquarters of the
Masons of California and the hub of Masonic activity in the state.
But below the Masonic temple, there’s another vital asset for the Masons
of California: the Nob Hill Masonic Center.
The NHMC operates a 565-stall parking garage that, in addition to serving
one of San Francisco’s busiest neighborhoods, plays a crucial role in supporting
the Masonic community’s fraternal and charitable endeavors and outreach programs, and helping fund the maintenance of the California Masonic Memorial
Temple. It is, in fact, a testament to the innovative thinking of the fraternity’s
leaders and one of the economic engines that powers the Masons of California.
As the only for-profit corporation of the Grand Lodge of California, the Nob
Hill Masonic Center is responsible for ensuring the efficient and effective operation of the California Masonic Memorial Temple garage in order to generate
an annual dividend for the Grand Lodge, which is its sole stockholder. In fiscal
year 2023, the NHMC achieved a historic milestone, with the Masonic garage
earning its highest-ever revenue, at more than $3 million—a testament to the
resilience and strategic planning of its leadership in the wake of the pandemic.
In addition, the NHMC board began leasing and operating the Grace Cathedral
parking lot, across California Street at 1051 Taylor Street, on January 1, 2022.
This year, that garage generated more than $800,000 in revenue, which, it is
important to note, is still approximately 20 percent behind pre-pandemic levels.
Faced with inflationary pressures affecting labor, insurance, maintenance,
and utilities costs, the Nob Hill Masonic Center projects net operating revenue exceeding $640,000, with after-tax profits expected to exceed $450,000.
This profit will meet the annual dividend requirement of the Grand Lodge of
California, ensuring the sustainability of this unique venture.
In recent years, the Nob Hill Masonic Center invested in several important
upgrades. The most recent example of these was the installation of new license
plate recognition equipment in 2023. This cutting-edge technology enhances
security and the overall customer experience. Every license plate entering
the facility is now recorded, ensuring a higher level of security. For added
convenience, paid customers exiting the garage no longer need to fumble for

218

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

a ticket; the system validates their entry and automatically raises the gate as
they approach to exit. Before that, a new Parking Access and Revenue Control
System was installed to provide more detailed management of ticketing and
receipts; and leased several parking stations to the electrical vehicle-charging
company Volta and added two DCFC supercharging stations.
Looking ahead to fiscal year 2024, the Nob Hill Masonic Center is finalizing
plans for new signage to enhance visibility and accessibility for patrons.
The center remains positive about the future, even as business in San
Francisco continues to recover slowly compared to other major U.S. cities. One
source of optimism is the recent amendment to the conditional use permit of
the CMMT, approved by the San Francisco Planning Commission. This amendment increases the annual number of live entertainment events permitted at the
Masonic from 79 to 91, promising positive impacts on its parking operations.
The Nob Hill Masonic Center extends its heartfelt thanks to Grand Master
Randy Brill and the entire executive committee for their unwavering support.
Grand Secretary Allan Casalou, who also serves as the center’s president and
chief executive, plays a vital role in its success. The Grand Lodge staff, including
Carol Hunter, Andy Cameron, and Khalil Sweidy, have been instrumental in the
center’s financial planning and business initiatives.
In closing, the Nob Hill Masonic Center is a shining example of how tradition and innovation can come together to support a noble cause. As it continues to adapt to changing times and grow, it remains a symbol of strength
within the Masons of California, upholding our heritage and commitment to
the community.
Respectfully submitted,

THE GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA
INSURANCE COMMITTEE REPORT
The Masons of California’s corporate insurance program provides
coverage for lodges, hall associations, the Masonic Homes, Acacia Creek, and
the California Masonic Memorial Temple (CMMT)/Nob Hill Masonic Center.
The program includes property, general liability, umbrella liability, earthquake,
D&O, employment practices liability, cyber liability, and crime insurance policies, all renewed April 1, 2023.
We continue as we ended last year’s insurance program, with a tough
renewal. By now we are all aware of the pressures on the insurance industry
with respect to insurers’ appetite for fire exposures. The result is a reduced
capacity to provide adequate limits and an overall increase in rates. Fire losses
are driving rate increases. On a positive note, our fire insurer has held deductibles at the same level for the last three years.
The grand lodge staff and the insurance committee felt it was time to
re-evaluate our relationship with the current broker, Marsh, and after a broker
selection process it was decided in early January to change brokers to Alliant
Insurance Brokers, which was felt would be in the best interest of grand lodge.
Grand lodge staff and the insurance committee worked diligently to look at
cost-saving areas as well as ideas beyond traditional insurance transactions.
These included self-insurance, insurance captives, and other risk-transfer methods. The committee will continue to review alternative risk-transfer methods.
Alliant reached out to insurance markets and wholesale brokers. Alliant
navigated a difficult marketplace, but we are confident that we identified the
most favorable coverages available to us.

REPORT OF THE
COMMITTEE ON INVESTMENT

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California
Executve Summary
The investment committee is charged with the prudent management
of the Grand Lodge investment fund (“GLIF”) with priority given to income
generation, capital preservation, and asset growth. The committee has adopted
a long-term target return of 6.75% annualized.
As of fiscal year, ending October 31st, 2023, the GLIF stands at approximately $911.7 million, and withdrawals by the Masonic entities during the
trailing twelve-months were in the amount of $87.6 million.
As of October 31st, 2023, the GLIF delivered a trailing twelve-months annualized return of 5.1% compared to the Allocation Index’s return of 5.6% over the
same period and the 6.75% long-term target return. The relative lower return
is mostly driven by the prevalent short-term volatility in the markets. To help
provide perspective and point of comparison, the GLIF trailing twelve-months
annualized return, as of September 30th, 2023, is 10.7%. Absent any major shifts,
the committee continues to believe that the current long-term investment
strategy has served the portfolio well in the past and should continue to do so.
Purpose
The investment committee is charged with the prudent management of GLIF.
The pool of assets invested is composed of the general and endowment funds
for the Masonic Home of California, investment funds of the California Masonic
Foundation, California Masonic Memorial Temple, and Grand Lodge. The
investment committee’s responsibilities and activities are governed by the
CMC sections 406.045, 407.040 B and D, and the approved Investment Policy
Statement (“IPS”).

The primary objective of the funds is to provide a regular and reliable source
of financial support to the Masonic entities or its beneficiaries, while preserving the purchasing power of the funds after reasonable withdrawals are taken.
Simply put, the investment objectives of the funds are income generation,
capital preservation, and asset growth. With that in mind, the committee has
adopted a long-term target return of 6.75% annualized.
Investment Selection & Monitoring
The committee is comprised of diligent financial professionals who are
astute in portfolio construction and global economics. NEPC, LLC., serves as
the committee’s investment consultant, which provides services in the areas
of identifying investment managers, due diligence, and modeling/evaluations.
The investment committee, with the assistance of NEPC, regularly identifies
and selects investment managers that have a higher probability of providing
incremental benefit to the overall Fund’s performance. This is accomplished
through global economic and markets analysis to identify appropriate asset
classes and allocation. Once the allocation is determined, individual managers
are selected utilizing data, research, and due diligence services provided by
NEPC. Once managers have been thoroughly vetted and consistently monitored, as long as the manager’s investment style is still part of the committee’s
investment thesis, it is relatively rare that a manager get terminated, unless the
committee have adjusted the positioning of the portfolio. This philosophy is
founded in the committee’s adopted IPS which states:
“We believe that manager turnover is very expensive and extremely disruptive to the efficiency and productive operation of an investment program.
Mangers should be hired with a long-run view… We also believe that the
constant and/or rapid turnover of managers, justified solely on the basis of
relative underperformance is usually an indication of a lack of adherence to
the selection and retention process. In particular, short-term (generally less
than one year) underperformance should not be a reason for termination,
unless it is accompanied by other adverse key retention characteristics.”
In monitoring the portfolio, the committee receives monthly performance
reports and meets quarterly. During these quarterly meetings, aside from discussing outstanding business or tactical decisions, regularly involve meetings
with one or two individual investment managers, review quarterly due diligence

230

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

and performance reports from NEPC. This allows the committee to monitor
the respective performance of the managers compared to various indices representing their objective. This process provides the committee with the necessary
data to evaluate each investment manager on a timely basis, and to observe
whether they continue to achieve the objectives of their mandate.

REPORT OF THE
COMMITTEE ON JURISPRUDENCE

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:
The committee on jurisprudence serves as the legal adviser to the grand
master and the legal adviser to the grand lodge when in session. The committee
reviews proposed resolutions and recommendations to be considered at the
next Annual Communication and prepares any necessary legislation to carry
out the intent of the proponents. At the Annual Communication, it comments
on the legality of the grand master’s decisions and dispensations and on the
legal effect of the proposed recommendations and resolutions. After the Annual
Communication, it prepares the changes to the California Masonic Code to reflect
the legislation which was adopted.
In the committee’s view, those of Grand Master Brill’s decisions and dispensations coming to its attention were legal and within his discretion. In the
committee’s view, the legislation posted by the grand secretary to the grand
lodge website on August 28 of this year is sufficient to carry out the intent of the
proponents, and the legislation contained in Grand Master Brill’s recommendation which he will present in his message is sufficient to carry out his intent.
We believe that each piece of this legislation has the legal effect set forth in it.
In presenting the legislation for your consideration, we make no recommendations as to the action to be taken with it. While the committee has written the
title and introductory explanation for each resolution before you and assisted
the proponents in drafting the code changes required to effect their intent, the
proponents’ arguments in their whereas clauses are their own. The committee
does not assist in drafting the whereas clauses and makes no comments on them.
The legislation posted by the grand secretary to the grand lodge website
on August 28 of this year and the legislation contained in Grand Master Brill’s
recommendation require no separate motion because they are automatically
before this Annual Communication. The presiding officer will announce the vote
required for the passage of each item before discussion begins. Any legislation
which does not amend the California Masonic Code or the ritual requires a simple
majority only for adoption. Any amendment to the California Masonic Code or
the ritual must be adopted by a five-sixths affirmative vote. If the amendment
receives a simple majority but less than a five-sixths affirmative vote, it carries

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

233

over to the next Annual Communication, when only a two-thirds affirmative
vote is required for adoption.
In addition to the foregoing responsibilities, the committee reviews all
charges and specifications of unmasonic conduct, strikes out those portions
which are not supported by a clear and precise specification of unmasonic conduct, and revises those portions which are incorrect, ambiguous, or insufficient.
The committee may dismiss charges if all the facts set forth in the specifications, even if true, would not warrant a verdict of unmasonic conduct. As part
of its review, the committee provides the parties with every essential factual
element which must be proven at trial for the accused to be found guilty of each
charge. Since the last Annual Communication, the committee commented on
the charges and specifications in 30 trials.
If a Mason under the disciplinary jurisdiction of this grand lodge has pleaded
guilty or nolo contendere (no contest) to, or has been convicted of, a crime of
moral turpitude by a federal or state court, he shall be deemed automatically
expelled from all the rights and privileges of Masonry without any further
action of his lodge or grand lodge. The committee reviews a certified copy of
the record of conviction to determine whether there has been an automatic
expulsion. Since the last Annual Communication, the committee has reviewed
eight federal or state court records to evaluate whether there has been an automatic expulsion of the Mason involved in the proceeding. These matters are
summarized in the attached exhibit.
No person shall hold or be eligible for membership in any constituent
lodge who has pleaded guilty or nolo contendere to, or has been convicted of, a
crime involving a violation of the moral law unless, for the reason that he did
not commit the offense, he either has been pardoned or had his judgment of
conviction vacated or reversed. All applicants are subject to background checks
to determine compliance with this rule. Since the last Annual Communication,
the grand secretary has not asked the committee to review any federal or state
court records to evaluate whether an applicant is eligible for the degrees.
We thank the grand master for the opportunity which he has given us to
serve this year.

California Masonic Code. An inherently evil intent is not required for a conviction
under Section 594(a)(b)(1) of the California Penal Code. Automatic expulsion
is not appropriate unless the only activity for which there could have been a
conviction under the applicable statute involves moral turpitude. Therefore,

Automatic Expulsions
October 19, 2022 to October 27, 2023
Trial No. 3005
In Trial No. 3005, the member pled guilty to a violation of California Penal Code
Section 273(a)(a) (the “Crime”). This Section provides that “any person who,
under circumstances or conditions likely to produce great bodily harm or death,
willfully causes or permits any child to suffer, or inflicts thereon unjustifiable
physical pain or mental suffering, or having the care or custody of any child,
willfully causes or permits the person or health of that child to be injured, or
willfully causes or permits that child to be placed in a situation where his or
her person or health is endangered, shall be punished by imprisonment in a
county jail not exceeding one year, or in the state prison for two, four, or six
years.” Under Section 100.075 of the California Masonic Code and 2009 Grand
Master’s Decision No. 2, assault with intent to commit serious bodily harm
involves moral turpitude. In the committee’s opinion, the conduct described in
California Penal Code Section 273(a)(a) involves assault with intent to commit
serious bodily harm. Therefore, based on the court record and the foregoing
analysis, it is the judgment of a majority of the members of the committee on
jurisprudence that the member pled guilty to a crime of moral turpitude before
a federal/state court. Accordingly, the member was automatically expelled from
all the rights and privileges of Masonry pursuant to Section 1404.820 of the
California Masonic Code. His expulsion from Masonry was effective on November
17, 2020, the date he entered his plea of guilty.
Trial No. 3017
In Trial No. 3017, the member pled guilty to a violation of California Penal Code
Section 594(a)(b)(1) (the “Crime”). This section provides that any person
“who maliciously commits any of the following acts with respect to any real
or personal property not of his or her own… is guilty of vandalism: (1) defaces
with graffiti or other inscribed material; (2) damages; (3) destroys…” Section
100.075 of the California Masonic Code and 2009 Grand Master’s Decision No. 2
provide guidance as to the meaning of the term of moral turpitude. It is the judgment of a majority of the members of the committee on jurisprudence that the
crime does not involve moral turpitude for purposes of Section 100.075 of the

235

Trial No. 3018
In Trial No. 3018, the member pled guilty to a violation of California Penal Code
Section 487(a) (the “Crime”). This section provides that “Grand theft is theft
committed… when the money, labor, real property, or personal property taken is
of a value exceeding nine hundred fifty dollars ($950)…” Under Section 100.075
of the California Masonic Code and 2009 Grand Master’s Decision No. 2, larceny
involves moral turpitude. In the committee’s opinion, the conduct described in
California Penal Code Section 487(a) involves larceny. Therefore, based on the
court record and the foregoing analysis, it is the judgment of a majority of the
members of the committee on jurisprudence that the member pled guilty to
a crime of moral turpitude before a state court. Accordingly, the member was
automatically expelled from all the rights and privileges of Masonry pursuant
to Section 1404.820 of the California Masonic Code. His expulsion from Masonry
was effective on September 11, 2018, the date he entered his plea of guilty.

The committee on Masonic properties is pleased to report that so far this

associations. Your committee is composed of residential and commercial real

managers, and insurance brokers.

our role and please be advised that your hall associations can reach out to the

Carry-over Legislation

Carry-over Resolution No. 22-02

Grand Master’s Recommendations
Recommendation No. 1
This recommendation seeks to amend the California Masonic Code (CMC)
to clarify certain lodge’s recognized anniversary dates.
Currently, CMC section 801.010 specifies that the anniversary of formation
date will be the date the grand master issued the dispensation, not the charter
date. The change in the code would state that the anniversary date be determined
by either the dispensation or charter date, whichever is earliest.
Many lodges in our jurisdiction were formed without being issued a dispensation by our grand lodge. Prior to the formation of California as a state
and our grand lodge in 1850, there were many lodges meeting in the territory
that were chartered by established grand lodges. A few months after our grand
lodge was formed, California became a state and as such the lodges that resided
within the new borders would ultimately apply for membership under the then
new Grand Lodge of Masons of California.
This recommendation would remove ambiguity for those lodges when
determining any of their future anniversary dates.

This resolution would authorize the grand master to confer the title of past
master upon a brother who served as master of his lodge but did not complete
his entire term because the lodge’s charter was suspended or revoked.
It would not require that the title of past master be conferred upon the
brother, but it would permit the grand master to investigate and contemplate
all of the circumstances of the situation, and to consider the circumstances of
other similar situations, in his consideration as to whether or not to confer the
past master title upon the brother.
The proponents assert that the suspension or revocation of a lodge’s charter might not be a reflection of the sitting master’s performance, and that he
may have served and performed admirably despite the lodge’s problems. They
contend that if the grand master determines this is the case, then he should
have the authority to acknowledge the brother’s service by conferring the past
master title upon him.
California Masonic Code (CMC) section 805.020 states the title of past
master applies only to a member who: (A) Has been regularly elected or named
in a charter as master of a chartered lodge; (B) Has been installed as master of
a chartered lodge; (C) Has served until the installation of his successor, except
in the case of death or consolidation as specified, or has served until reinstalled
as master for the subsequent year; and (D) Is at the time in good standing.
This resolution would amend CMC section 805.020 to give the grand master
the discretion to confer the title upon a brother who did not serve until the
installation of his successor because the lodge’s charter was suspended, and he
was removed from office or the lodge’s charter was revoked.
This resolution would not impose any time limitations on the conferral
of the past master title by the grand master, nor would it limit the number
of times a request to confer the past master title could be submitted to the
grand master or succeeding grand masters. This would allow requests to be
made to grand masters several years down the road who may not be familiar with the facts and circumstances at the time and after memories have
somewhat faded. Furthermore, it could result in a scenario wherein successive grand masters, year after year, are lobbied to confer the past master
title upon the brother until some grand master eventually says “yes.”
Additionally, this resolution could disrupt the peace and harmony within the

242

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

lodge. For example, the grand master might confer the past master title on a
brother when his lodge believes him undeserving, or vice versa. Additionally,
as the resolution is written, the grand master’s decision on whether or not to
confer the past master title would not be subject to the review or approval of
the grand lodge.
There are social and other benefits to being a past master. A past master
is eligible to cast the collective vote of the past masters of his lodge at annual
communication per CMC section 403.075. He continues to be addressed as
“Worshipful” after he completes his term. He may receive gifts, such as an
apron, a life membership, or some other honorarium from his lodge. It is entirely
understandable that a brother who diligently executed his duties as a lodge
master would want to be acknowledged as a past master for his service, even
if his lodge’s charter was revoked or suspended through no fault of his own.
Traditionally, if a master has been removed from office or the lodge’s charter
has been revoked before he completes his first term, he has not been entitled to
the title of past master. It is for this grand lodge to decide whether the benefits
afforded by this resolution to a master who would otherwise not qualify as a
past master should be adopted.
At Annual Communication in 2022, the grand lodge passed Grand Master’s
Decision No. 1, an interpretive decision which clarified that a lodge master
may not receive the title of past master if he does not complete his term or
serve until the installation of his successor. If this resolution passes, the Grand
Master’s Decision will be rendered moot because the CMC will be updated by
the resolution, and this resolution would then govern.

required to complete the project, warranty terms, and contractors’ certificate of
insurance as well as other applicable insurance required to complete the project.
Proponents contend that monetary inflation has increased the costs for
services that in the past would have been under the current threshold. The
$25,000 threshold was adopted in the year 2000, which adjusted for inflation,
approximates to $43,000 in today’s dollars.
Proponents also assert that this resolution would likely reduce the amount
of submissions to the committee, allowing for more expeditious approval of
needed repairs, and avoiding further expenses from rising cost of labor and
materials. The committee maintains a 10-day response time per submission.
Further delay may result if a Masonic hall association does not submit required
documentation for review in a timely manner. Of 256 Masonic hall associations
in the last five years, Masonic Properties received 45 applications for improvement. Of those applications, fewer than 22 were under $50,000. Over the last
five years, that averages to fewer than five applications per year for improvements under $50,000.
Many brothers elected to Masonic hall associations by constituent lodges do
not have experience in hiring contractors for large-scale building improvements.
The duty of the committee on Masonic properties is to provide such expertise
via legal analysis to ensure contracts for improvements are written appropriately
and cover important details, such as properly defining the involved parties, the
scope of work, insurance requirements, and any appropriate legal remedies in
the event of breach of contract. Failure to seek appropriate counsel from the
committee has resulted in financial harm to lodges and hall associations without
recourse. Additionally, the committee reviews the overall financial standing
of the lodge or hall association, to ensure adequate capital is available in the
event of unforeseen additional costs. The committee has experienced many
situations in which a lodge or hall association has over-extended its financial
abilities when entering a contract for a given project.
It is up to this voting body to determine whether the convenience of not
consulting the committee on Masonic properties on projects under $50,000 is
worth the additional financial and legal risks.

Carry-over Resolution No. 22-04
This resolution would increase the threshold amount of a contract requiring
approval from the Grand Lodge Committee on Masonic Properties. Specifically,
this resolution would amend the California Masonic Code (CMC) section
406.060(D) to state $50,000 instead of $25,000.
The CMC currently requires the committee on Masonic properties to examine and approve all details regarding any contract involving a lodge, Masonic hall
association, committee, partnership or corporation, or other entity representing
itself to be Masonic in character, or operating for the benefit of a lodge or lodges
in this jurisdiction, for a contract for or commencement of the construction,
alteration, improvement, replacement, repair or other maintenance of real
property if the expected cost is in excess of $25,000.
Hall associations are not allowed to re-classify a project into a series of
smaller projects for the purpose of keeping costs under the $25,000 threshold
in the same budgetary year.
The committee on Masonic properties requires, at the time of application,
minutes of the lodge or hall association containing the approval for the project, current lodge or hall association bank statements, three competitive bids,

Resolution No. 23-02

New Resolutions for 2023
Resolution 23-01
The proponents of this resolution seek to allow lodges to send minutes to
members by electronic mail.
This resolution would amend California Masonic Code (CMC) sections
805.230 and 807.030 to permit electronic distribution of lodge minutes to lodge
members prior to the stated meeting at which those minutes would be required
to be read. Upon successful appropriate motion, the reading of the minutes that
have been so distributed could be waived and the minutes adopted. The monitor would also require a revision as the new language would be included in it.
Prior distribution of the minutes may give lodge members more time to
review and potentially correct them, resulting in more accurate record keeping for lodges. The draft minutes must be provided 72 hours prior to the next
stated meeting. Waiving the reading of minutes may shorten the length of stated
meetings. Recently our jurisdiction has amended sections of our CMC to allow
for the use of new technology, such as Zoom or Google Meet, if all security and
privacy policies are met to conduct limited lodge business. Conversely, distributing lodge communications to members via e-mail might see those minutes
inadvertently distributed to unintended parties, or appropriated by third party
bad actors. Not being able to review the waived minutes prior to signature could
lead to an inadvertent or willful substitution of the distributed minutes with
a different draft. It is noted that the legislation does not contain any verbiage
relative to maintaining lodge confidentiality.
This resolution creates a choice rather than a mandate for the lodges. If
authorized by a standing resolution of the lodge, the secretary shall provide
electronically all minutes of meetings of the lodge to the electronic mail address
of record for each Mason of the lodge. Any objection to the motion, or vote
that is not unanimous to waive reading, automatically causes the minutes to
be required reading at the stated meeting. It is up to the members of this grand
lodge to decide if they trust the secretaries and brethren with the veracity of
the minutes, their diligence in secure distribution, and all brothers’ sworn duty
to maintain confidentiality.

This resolution would amend California Masonic Code (CMC) section 811.010 to
permit a Master Mason to be installed as secretary of more than one constituent
lodge at the same time.
The proponents of this resolution assert that:
1.

It can take years for a new secretary to learn the job effectively

2.

Experienced secretaries are hard to find

3.

It is particularly difficult to fill a vacancy in the office of secretary for
smaller and more remote lodges

4.

Some of the duties of secretary can now be done electronically, lessening the time required to perform such duties

CMC section 811.010 states a member may not be master, warden, or secretary, or any combination thereof, of two or more lodges (other than research
lodges and historic lodges) at the same time. No member may hold more than
one office in a lodge at the same time.
This resolution would not set a maximum number of lodges in which a
member may serve as secretary, nor would it amend CMC section 805.230
to provide the maximum pay a member may receive from one or more of the
lodges he serves as secretary.
This resolution would not amend CMC section 809.550(k) to determine
responsibility for a shared secretary’s annual dues for membership in a Masonic
secretaries’ association and the reasonable expenses of that association including the cost of meals. As such expenditures are considered discretionary, there
may be conflict between constituent lodges in determining the appropriate
portion, if any, for which each lodge shall be responsible.
This resolution would only amend California Masonic Code section 811.010
to permit a Master Mason to be installed as secretary of more than one constituent lodge at the same time.
Resolution No. 23-03
Section 807.010 of the California Masonic Code (CMC) expressly prohibits lodges
from holding a special meeting on the same day as a stated meeting. The proponents of this resolution seek to amend that section to give lodges the right to
hold one or more special meetings on the same day as a stated meeting. Under
this resolution, while a lodge would be able to hold a special meeting on the
same day as a stated meeting, a lodge would not be allowed to hold a special
meeting at the same time as the stated meeting. Similarly, a lodge would not be
allowed to hold two or more special meetings at the same time. This resolution
is permissive only and does not require lodges to hold other meetings on the
day of the stated meeting. This resolution does not change any of the other

246

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

247

requirements applicable to special meetings or stated meetings under the CMC.
If this resolution were adopted, lodges could benefit from having more
flexibility in the scheduling of their meetings. As the proponents noted, lodges
in remote areas often have members traveling long distances to attend meetings
and the ability to have one or more special meetings on the same day as the
stated meeting would decrease the number of times those members would have
to make such long journeys. It is possible that smaller lodges, and even lodges
whose members have busy work or family schedules, could likewise benefit
from consolidating their meeting dates.
Having one or more special meetings on the day of the stated meeting
could increase the number of degrees or other activities that a lodge could
accomplish in any given month. However, it would also mean that members
would be at lodge for several hours on the stated meeting day, which could
lead to member fatigue as some lodges have a limited number of members with
the ability or necessary qualifications to fulfill certain roles. If this resolution
is adopted, lodges should exercise its ability to hold multiple meetings on the
stated meeting day judiciously.
It is for this voting body to decide whether lodges having the ability to hold
one or more special meetings on the same day as the stated meeting would be of
sufficient benefit to the fraternity to warrant the proposed changes to the code.

La France Lodge U.D. has completed all of the requirements to obtain its
charter and it will be approved at this Annual Communication. The new lodge,
La France Lodge No. 885, has sufficient French-speaking members to perform
the traditional French Masonic ritual.
There are two lodges in California performing the first degree in French
using a French style of ritual. La Parfaite Union Lodge No. 17 in San Francisco
and Vallee de France No. 329 in Pasadena. With the consolidation of Vallee de
France, there would not be a French-speaking lodge in the southern half of
the state.
Vallee de France No. 329 sent a letter to grand lodge in support of La France
Lodge being given the right to work its degrees using the traditional French
Masonic ritual previously used by Vallee de France Lodge. La France Lodge is
currently meeting in the city of Santa Monica, which is on the west side of Los
Angeles.
Approval of this resolution will add the following words to section 402.010
of the CMC: “The right to perform the long-established ritualistic work of Vallee
de France Lodge No. 329 has been transferred to and assumed by La France
Lodge with the requisite approval of Grand Lodge.”
The granting of this right to La France Lodge can only be approved by
amending the CMC, therefore it requires your approval.

Resolution No. 23-04

Resolution No. 23-05

The proponents of this resolution seek to amend section 402.010 of the California
Masonic Code (CMC) to allow La France Lodge U.D. to work its degrees using
the traditional French Masonic ritual previously approved to be used by Vallee
de France Lodge No. 329.
Section 402.010 of the CMC is titled RITUAL, and requires all work in this
jurisdiction, including each degree conferred and all lectures, to be in conformity
with the ritual, and as such must be adhered to by all lodges and Masons in
this jurisdiction, except as otherwise provided in this code. Constituent lodges
whose long-established ritualistic work is in part a departure from the ritual of
this jurisdiction may continue to perform such ritual, for so long as the same
has not been disapproved by action of the grand master and the grand lecturer.
Vallee de France Lodge No. 329 is one of the lodges with a long-established
ritualistic work referred to in section 402.010 of the CMC. They have, since
1897, been a French-speaking lodge performing the first degree in French using
a French style of ritual previously approved by grand lodge. Vallee de France is
no longer able to perform the degrees due to a lack of French-speaking members.
In fact, Vallee de France No. 329 is consolidating with Round Table Lodge No.
876. That consolidation should be approved at this Annual Communication.
The new consolidated lodge will not have sufficient French-speaking members
required for the degree. Therefore, the consolidated lodge must perform all of
its work in conformity with the ritual of the Grand Lodge of California.

Currently, California Masonic Code (“CMC”) section 403.075 allows past masters collectively of each chartered lodge to one vote only. The proponents of
this resolution seek to modify CMC section 403.075(d) to read,
• A Designated Past Master may cast the vote of the Past Masters
collectively of a constituent Lodge at an Annual Communication if a
specific Past Master is chosen to do so by such Lodge as provided in
this section.
• The Designated Past Master may be chosen by either those members of the Lodge or by those Past Masters of the Lodge, present and
voting at a Stated Meeting as the Lodge may determine.
• The Lodge Master with the attest of the Lodge Secretary shall certify
to the Grand Secretary the Lodge’s Designated Past Master, if any, for
the applicable Annual Communication.
• If a chartered Lodge has chosen a Designated Past Master such
Designated Past Master shall have the sole right to collect the
Past Master’s ballot for such Lodge for the applicable Annual
Communication.
The proponents of this resolution seek to address a problem some lodges are

248

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

facing with a past master collecting the ballot and not exercising the collective
vote of the past masters present. If this resolution were passed, it would not
be mandatory for lodges to do this. Lodges would have to vote first on whether
or not to designate a past master. If they choose to designate a past master,
they will have to determine whether to vote by all members or by a vote of past
masters. They would have to use that method to designate a past master. They
would have to get the master’s signature and attest of the lodge secretary in
time to get that designation to the grand secretary in sufficient time to restrict
the ballot to that past master. As proposed, this would have to be done on an
annual basis
There are some problems with the language of this resolution. The resolution does not state the manner in which notice would be provided to its members
to ensure all those desiring to participate in the balloting can be present. The
resolution does not address the issue of what would happen if the designated
past master failed to attend Annual Communication as the resolution restricts
the voting right to that one designated past master. The language in the resolution that the “designated past master may be chosen by either those members
of the lodge or by those past masters of the lodge as the lodge may determine”
may lead to disharmony between past masters and members.
The lodge would have sole authority for which group would be entitled to
make this election, thereby potentially turning this decision-making process
into an issue of personalities (members verses past masters) and could open
the door for politicking and could lead to lodge unrest.
It is up to this voting body to decide whether or not this issue and this
resolution requires an amendment to the CMC.

The legislation, as presented, is likely to result in confusion if adopted. It does not
change when an individual become a member of a lodge nor change when they qualify for either the Golden Veteran or Diamond Jubilee awards under section 408.010.
“Years of service” is not a standard used under any part of the CMC. The most
expedient means of achieving the perceived purpose of the proposed legislation would be the elimination of the informational field to which offense is

REPORT OF THE
COMMITTEE ON TRIAL REVIEW

Brethren,
Your committee on trial review has carefully examined the records of
all cases completed during this Masonic year. Unless otherwise noted, in each
of the matters, the committee finds that there was compliance with the procedural requirements of the California Masonic Code. Unless otherwise noted,
all of the committee’s decisions were by a unanimous vote of the members of
the committee.
The committee emphasizes that charges of unmasonic conduct against a
brother Mason are serious. They subject the brother, the lodge, and concordant
and appendant bodies to disharmony. Every effort should be made by the accuser
and others to avoid filing charges against a brother and every effort should be
made to seek settlement or mediation at the earliest opportunity.
The committee also emphasizes that no brother should submit charges
of unmasonic conduct against a brother Mason which are based, in whole or
in part, on speculation. Charges should only be filed against a brother after it
has been fully investigated and the accuser can establish by a preponderance
of the evidence each required element of the charge. The filing of ill-conceived
charges not only harms the accused but the accuser and the fraternal family.
In Case No. 3002, one committee member recused himself. The accuser
alleged two charges against the accused alleging that he embezzled rent due
from an appendant body to the hall association for a period of years. The accuser
also alleged a charge of drinking a beer during a remote, virtual meeting and
a charge for using the chairs of the social hall for a personal party while the
building was closed.
The accused, a retired law enforcement officer, a past master, a Hiram Award
recipient, an officer of the hall association, and an officer of the appendant body,
emphatically denied that he had embezzled any funds.
At the pretrial conference, the trial master confirmed with the accuser that,
as he had admitted in his charges, he did not have any of the financial records
from the appendant body. These financial records were necessary to confirm
the alleged embezzlement of funds.
The charges involving the accused’s consumption of a beer during a virtual

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

251

meeting and the use of the social hall chairs while the building was closed were
withdrawn by the accuser.
During the pretrial conference, the accused represented, and it was confirmed, that the appendant body had provided its financial records to the president of the hall association. The president was holding the records and awaiting
an order from the trial master.
Rather than dismiss the case at the pretrial conference, the trial master
ordered that the financial records of the hall association and the appendant body
be audited by a Master Mason agreed upon between the parties. Accordingly,
the parties were ordered to mediate the matter until the question of embezzlement was resolved.
The parties’ agreed upon third-party Master Mason, with an extensive
background in financial auditing, reviewed the records and found that there was
no evidence of embezzlement. The accuser agreed with the third-party Mason’s
findings and apologized to the accused. Consequently, the parties entered into
an agreement of factual innocence of the accused. Based on the agreement of
factual innocence, the trial master then found the accused factually innocent
based on the agreed facts stipulated to by the parties and dismissed the charges.
Members of the trial review committee, other than the recused member, upheld
the trial master’s finding of factual innocence based on the agreed facts of the
parties and dismissal of the charges.
The committee therefore submits and moves that the following resolution
be adopted: Resolved, that in Case No. 3002, the trial master’s finding of
factual innocence and dismissal of the charges after mediation be affirmed.
The resolution was adopted.
In case No. 2791, one committee member recused himself. The accused,
who was a licensed contractor, was charged with unmasonic conduct arising out
of an incident in which he physically assaulted the owner of the property who
was an Entered Apprentice of the same lodge. The assault resulted in criminal
charges being filed and initially prosecuted against the accused.
In addition to the criminal proceeding, there were several civil and administrative proceedings filed by the parties against each other. Accordingly, the
trial master stayed the Masonic proceedings pending the completion of the
civil and criminal matters.
The criminal matter was terminated by the accused’s agreement to enter
and complete a diversion program in anger management. While the civil matters
were still proceeding, the accused continued to engage in unmasonic conduct
which included false and derogatory statements against the Entered Apprentice
threatening his professional license and employment; false, defamatory, foul
and abusive language; and other threatening conduct directed toward the trial
master and his family; and defamatory and threatening conduct toward the
witnesses, including numerous Master Masons.

252

P r o c e e di ng s of t h e

G r a n d L od g e F. & A . M . of C a l i f or n i a

Upon conclusion of the civil proceedings, the trial master ordered the
accused to serve his formal response to the charges of unmasonic conduct. The
accused failed to submit the formal response, and the trial master commenced
his investigation.
The accused later claimed to the trial master to have timely served a formal
response and contended that the trial master was intentionally being dishonest
stating this is “f___ Bull___”.
Despite the statements, the trial master offered the accused an opportunity
to establish that he had timely submitted the formal response in compliance
with the trial master’s orders. Instead, the accused submitted an email which was
not credible and not in compliance with the trial master’s order. The attached
formal response also failed to comply with the Masonic Code and in place of
his signature at one point the accused had inserted “So f____ you!”
Accordingly, the trial master proceeded with his investigation. During the
investigation, the accused continued to engage in misconduct intended to frustrate the trial master’s investigation, including attempting to extort witnesses
and the accuser; used fraudulent and threatening behavior directed toward
the trial master; and the pursuit of false and defamatory claims against anyone
connected to the proceedings.
Despite the accused’s attempts to frustrate the investigation and the imposition of the penalty, the trial master found that the physical assault had taken
place and was part and parcel of significant misconduct which violated the
moral law and accordingly found the accused guilty. Due to the consistent and
regular violations of the moral law, he affixed the penalty at expulsion. Members
of the trial review committee, other than the one recused member, upheld the
trial master’s decision.

matter be returned to the trial master for proper service in accordance
with the California Masonic Code.
The resolution was adopted.

The committee therefore submits and moves that the following resolution
be adopted: Resolved, that in Case No. 2792, the trial master’s findings,
verdict and penalty of expulsion be affirmed.
The resolution was adopted.
In case No. 2793, the accused was charged with breach of fiduciary duty,
theft, embezzlement, and fraud for mishandlings in his employment as a hall
association building manager. The accused failed to respond to the specification
of charges, and the trial master found the accused guilty after conducting an
investigation, imposing a penalty of expulsion.
Upon review of the record by the committee on trial review, it was determined that the accused was not served in the manner mandated by the California
Masonic Code.
The committee on trial review therefore submits and moves for the adoption of the following resolution: Resolved that in case No. 2793 that the
decision of the trial master and penalty of expulsion be set aside, and the

253

In Case No. 3001, the accused was charged with breach of fiduciary duty
and fraud related to negotiations for improvements to the hall. The accused
plead not guilty to the charges. The accuser was unable to substantiate or
provide any evidence in support of the accusations. The trial master found
no evidence in support of the charges and accordingly found the accused not
guilty. Upon review of the record, the committee on trial review noted that there
were numerous questions of fact and a majority of the committee determined
that based upon the failure of the accuser to present any evidence against the
accused, the verdict should be changed from “not guilty” to “a dismissal of the
charges without prejudice.”
The committee therefore submits and moves that the following resolution
be adopted: Resolved, that in Case No. 3001, the trial master’s findings be
affirmed but that the verdict be changed from “not guilty” to a dismissal
of the charges without prejudice.
The resolution was adopted.
The following case involves a previously expelled member who has requested
restoration of Masonic membership:
In Case No. 2657, Jolan Pascua was expelled in 2015 for striking the senior
warden of his lodge during an argument. In 2021, he applied for restoration and
because the committee on trial review determined that his prior application
was deficient in a number of respects, it recommended a “no” vote, which
grand lodge accepted.
He has again applied for restoration, this time expressing his unequivocal
remorse for his actions, submitting proof that in the intervening eight years
he has been laboring for the benefit of his two lodges, has apologized to the
victim and received his forgiveness, even submitting a picture of them together
and stated that the personal problems which caused his behavior have been
rectified. Both of his previous lodges overwhelmingly voted for restoration of
his membership.
Considering all of the above, the committee on trial review determined
that Mr. Pascua has substantially complied with the mandates of Grand Master
Adamson’s Decision No. 3, listing the factors to be considered for restoration.
The committee on trial review therefore submits and moves the adoption
of the following resolution: Resolved that in case No. 2657, as to Mr. Jolan
Pascua, his application to grand lodge for restoration be granted and he
be restored to the rights and privileges of Masonry.
The resolution was adopted.
